For the more general definition, we introduce the notion of a partition of the random vector ${ \overline { { Y } } } = \left( { Y _ { 1 } , Y _ { 2 } , \dots , Y _ { n } } \right)$ into two nonempty subsets of random variables ${ \overline { { Y } } } _ { 1 } = ( Y _ { j _ { 1 } } , Y _ { j _ { 2 } } , \ldots , Y _ { j _ { m } } )$ , and ${ \overline { { Y } } } _ { 2 } = ( Y _ { i _ { 1 } } , Y _ { i _ { 2 } } , \dots , Y _ { i _ { n - m } } )$ , where this cumbersome notation is intended to imply that every $Y _ { k }$ is in one of $\overline { { Y } } _ { 1 }$ and $\overline { { Y } } _ { 2 }$ but not both. 

Definition 7.31 Given a random vector ${ \overline { { Y } } } = \left( { Y _ { 1 } , Y _ { 2 } , \dots , Y _ { n } } \right)$ on a discrete sample space, $s ,$ an associated joint probability distribution function $f ( y _ { 1 } , y _ { 2 } , \ldots , y _ { n } )$ , and a partition, $\overline { { \boldsymbol { Y } } } = \left( \overline { { \boldsymbol { Y } } } _ { 1 } , \overline { { \boldsymbol { Y } } } _ { 2 } \right)$ , the marginal probability density function, denoted $f ( { \overline { { y } } } _ { 1 } )$ is defined by 

$$
f (\bar {y} _ {1}) = \sum_ {\bar {y} _ {2}} f (y _ {1}, y _ {2}, \dots , y _ {n}).\tag{7.30}
$$

The associated conditionalprobability densityfunction, denoted $f ( \overline { { y } } _ { 2 } | \overline { { y } } _ { 1 } )$ , is defined by 

$$
f (\bar {y} _ {2} \mid \bar {y} _ {1}) = \frac {f (y _ {1} , y _ {2} , \dots , y _ {n})}{f (\bar {y} _ {1})} \quad \text { when } f (\bar {y} _ {1}) \neq 0.\tag{7.31}
$$

We note that these general formulas also provide general versions of the law of total probability, but leave it to the reader to develop these formulas. 

## 7.4.5 Independent Random Variables

Because a random variable X is defined so that the pre-image of open intervals $X ^ { - 1 } [ ( a , b ) ]$ are events in $\mathcal { E }$ with associated probabilities under the probability measure 

Pr, it is natural to say that two random variables are independent if their pre-images of all intervals are stochastically independent as events in E. 

Definition 7.32 Random variables $X _ { 1 } , ~ X _ { 2 }$ on the discrete sample space S are independent random variables if for any intervals $( a _ { j } , b _ { j } ) \subset \mathbb { R }$ , bounded or unbounded, $X _ { 1 } ^ { - 1 } [ ( a _ { 1 } , b _ { 1 } ) ]$ and $X _ { 2 } ^ { - 1 } [ ( a _ { 2 } , b _ { 2 } ) ]$ are stochastically independent events in E as in (7.5). Equivalently, if $X _ { 1 } : { \mathcal { S } }  \{ x _ { 1 j } \}$ and $X _ { 2 } : { \mathcal { S } }  \{ x _ { 2 k } \}$ , then $X _ { 1 }$ and $X _ { 2 }$ are independent $i f \ X _ { 1 } ^ { - 1 } [ x _ { 1 j } ]$ and $X _ { 2 } ^ { - 1 } [ x _ { 2 k } ]$ are stochastically independent events for all $x _ { 1 j }$ and $x _ { 2 k }$ 

More generally, a collection of random variables $\{ X _ { j } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { n }$ , where n may be <sub>y</sub>, are mutually independent random variables if every collection of events of the form $\{ X _ { j } ^ { - 1 } [ ( a _ { j } , b _ { j } ) ] \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { n }$ are mutually independent events as in (7.6), or equivalently, $\{ \bar { X _ { j } ^ { - 1 } } [ x _ { j k } ] \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { n }$ are mutually independent for any $x _ { j k } \in \mathbf { R } \mathbf { n g } [ X _ { j } ]$ 

## Example 7.33

1. Define S as the sample space of all pairs of results achieved by rolling a fair die twice. Specifically, $S = \{ ( d _ { 1 } , d _ { 2 } ) | 1 \leq d _ { j } \leq 6 \}$ , where $d _ { 1 }$ denotes the result on the first roll, and $d _ { 2 }$ the result on the second. By the assumption of fairness, each numerical value is equally likely and has probability $o f \frac { 1 } { 6 }$ of occurrence, and consequently the probability function for S is defined as $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { P r } [ ( d _ { 1 } , \stackrel { \cdot } { d } _ { 2 } ) ] = \frac { 1 } { 3 6 } } \end{array}$ for every such sample point. Note that the values of this probability measure are influenced by the fact that the die throws were sequential, and hence order counts. On this ordered sample space, define first the random variables $X , Y : S  \mathbb { N } b y$ 

$$
X [ (d _ {1}, d _ {2}) ] = d _ {1},
$$

$$
Y [ (d _ {1}, d _ {2}) ] = d _ {2}.
$$

Intuition indicates that X and Y are independent random variables. To demonstrate this, note that for any $d _ { 1 } , d _ { 2 } \in \{ 1 , 2 , \ldots , 6 \}$ , both $X ^ { - 1 } ( d _ { 1 } )$ and $Y ^ { - 1 } ( d _ { 2 } )$ are events in $\mathcal { S }$ of 6 points with measures under Pr of <sup>1</sup> . Also $X ^ { - 1 } ( d _ { 1 } ) \cap Y ^ { - 1 } ( d _ { 2 } )$ contains a unique sample point, specifically, $( d _ { 1 } , d _ { 2 } )$ , which has measure $\frac { 1 } { 3 6 }$ under Pr. In other words, for all $( d _ { 1 } , d _ { 2 } )$ ， 

$$
\operatorname * {P r} \left[ X ^ {- 1} \left(d _ {1}\right) \cap Y ^ {- 1} \left(d _ {2}\right) \right] = \operatorname * {P r} \left[ X ^ {- 1} \left(d _ {1}\right) \right] \operatorname * {P r} \left[ Y ^ {- 1} \left(d _ {2}\right) \right].
$$

2. Now define a new random variable Z on S above as follows: 

$$
Z [ (d _ {1}, d _ {2}) ] = d _ {1} + d _ {2}.
$$

Intuitively we expect X and Z not to be independent. That is because, $i f Z [ ( d _ { 1 } , d _ { 2 } ) ] =$ $1 2 \ ( o r \ 2 )$ , it must be the case that $X [ ( d _ { 1 } , d _ { 2 } ) ] = 6 ~ ( o r ~ 1 )$ . More formally, Z assumes all integer values $2 \leq k \leq 1 2$ , and the event defined by $Z ^ { - 1 } ( k )$ has probabilities 

<table><tr><td>k:</td><td>2</td><td>3</td><td>4</td><td>5</td><td>6</td><td>7</td><td>8</td><td>9</td><td>10</td><td>11</td><td>12</td></tr><tr><td><eq>\Pr[Z^{-1}(k)]</eq>:</td><td><eq>\frac{1}{36}</eq></td><td><eq>\frac{2}{36}</eq></td><td><eq>\frac{3}{36}</eq></td><td><eq>\frac{4}{36}</eq></td><td><eq>\frac{5}{36}</eq></td><td><eq>\frac{6}{36}</eq></td><td><eq>\frac{5}{36}</eq></td><td><eq>\frac{4}{36}</eq></td><td><eq>\frac{3}{36}</eq></td><td><eq>\frac{2}{36}</eq></td><td><eq>\frac{1}{36}</eq></td></tr></table>

It is apparent that the numerator of $\operatorname* { P r } [ Z ^ { - 1 } ( k ) ]$ also represents the number of sample points in the associated event. As noted above, for each $1 \leq j \leq 6 , X ^ { - 1 } ( j )$ contains 6 sample points, and $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { P r } [ X ^ { - 1 } ( j ) ] = \frac { 1 } { 6 } } \end{array}$ for all j. Now it is straightforward to justify that $X ^ { - 1 } ( j ) \cap Z ^ { - 1 } ( k )$ contains one sample point or none. For example, $X ^ { - 1 } ( 1 ) \cap Z ^ { - 1 } ( 1 2 )$ $= \emptyset .$ , while $X ^ { - 1 } ( 4 ) \cap Z ^ { - 1 } ( 7 ) = ( 4 , 3 )$ . More generally, if $d _ { \mathrm { l } } = j$ and $d _ { 1 } + d _ { 2 } = k _ { 3 }$ there is a unique point provided that $1 \le k - j \le 6 .$ and no point otherwise. Hence $\operatorname* { P r } [ X ^ { - 1 } ( j ) \cap Z ^ { - 1 } ( k ) ]$ equals $0 \ o r \ { \frac { 1 } { 3 6 } }$ , which can equal the product of probabilities of the respective events only when $k = 7 .$ . Consequently X and Z are not independent. 

3. Ifinstead ofas in case 1, a pair ofdice were thrown without keeping track oforder, then the sample space, ${ \mathbf { } } S ^ { \prime } { \mathrm { , } }$ , would contain only 21 rather than 36 sample points. One realization of this space is $\mathcal { S } ^ { \prime } = \{ ( d _ { 1 } , d _ { 2 } ) | 1 \leq d _ { 1 } \leq d _ { 2 } \leq 6 \}$ where $d _ { 1 }$ denotes the smaller result, $d _ { 2 }$ the larger. The associated probability measure is then given by 

$$
\operatorname * {P r} [ (d _ {1}, d _ {2}) ] = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \frac {1}{3 6} & d _ {1} = d _ {2}, \\ \frac {1}{1 8} & d _ {1} <   d _ {2}. \end{array} \right.
$$

Define the random variables $U , W : S ^ { \prime } \to \mathbb { N } b y$ 

$$
U [ (d _ {1}, d _ {2}) ] = \min (d _ {1}, d _ {2}),
$$

$$
W [ (d _ {1}, d _ {2}) ] = \max (d _ {1}, d _ {2}).
$$

Now U and W are not independent. For example, $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { P r } [ U ^ { - 1 } ( 1 ) ] = \frac { 1 1 } { 3 6 } } \end{array}$ , since this event contains the sample point 

$$
U ^ {- 1} (1) = \{(1, d) \mid 1 \leq d \leq 6 \},
$$

which has measure ${ \begin{array} { l } { { \frac { 1 1 } { 3 6 } } } \end{array} } b y$ the above given probability measure on $\mathcal { S } ^ { \prime } .$ . On the other hand, $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { P r } [ W ^ { - 1 } ( 1 ) ] = \frac { 1 } { 3 6 } } \end{array}$ , since $W ^ { - 1 } ( 1 ) = ( 1 , 1 )$ . Also $U ^ { - 1 } ( 1 ) \cap W ^ { - 1 } ( 1 ) = W ^ { - 1 } ( 1 )$ Consequently 

$$
\operatorname * {P r} [ U ^ {- 1} (1) \cap W ^ {- 1} (1) ] \neq \operatorname * {P r} [ U ^ {- 1} (1) ] \operatorname * {P r} [ W ^ {- 1} (1) ].
$$

The notion of independent random variables can also be defined in terms of the joint, conditional and marginal probability distribution functions. 

Definition 7.34 Given a random vector $\overline { { Y } } = \left( Y _ { 1 } , Y _ { 2 } \right)$ on a discrete sample space $\mathcal { S }$ and associated joint probability density function $f ( y _ { 1 } , y _ { 2 } )$ , the random variables $Y _ { 1 }$ and $Y _ { 2 }$ are independent random variables $i f$ 

$$
f (y _ {1}, y _ {2}) = f (y _ {1}) f (y _ {2}),\tag{7.32a}
$$

or equivalently $i f f ( y _ { 2 } ) \neq 0 .$ 

$$
f (y _ {1} \mid y _ {2}) = f (y _ {1}).\tag{7.32b}
$$

More generally, given a random vector ${ \overline { { Y } } } = \left( { Y _ { 1 } , Y _ { 2 } , \dots , Y _ { n } } \right)$ on the discrete sample space ${ \mathcal { S } } ,$ with associated joint probability density function $f ( y _ { 1 } , y _ { 2 } , \ldots , y _ { n } )$ , the random variables $\{ Y _ { j } \}$ are mutually independent random variables if given any partition $\overline { { Y } } = \left( \overline { { Y } } _ { 1 } , \overline { { Y } } _ { 2 } \right)$ 

$$
f (y _ {1}, y _ {2}, \dots , y _ {n}) = f (\overline {{Y}} _ {1}) f (\overline {{Y}} _ {2}),\tag{7.33a}
$$

or equivalently $i f f ( \overline { { Y } } _ { 2 } ) \neq 0 .$ 

$$
f (\overline {{Y}} _ {1} \mid \overline {{Y}} _ {2}) = f (\overline {{Y}} _ {1}).\tag{7.33b}
$$

In particular, we then have 

$$
f (y _ {1}, y _ {2}, \dots , y _ {n}) = f (y _ {1}) f (y _ {2}) \dots f (y _ {n}).\tag{7.34}
$$

## 7.5 Expectations of Discrete Distributions

## 7.5.1 Theoretical Moments

The definitions and notation for moments here closely parallel that given in section 3.3.2 for moments of sample data. This is no coincidence, as will be discussed below. 

## Expected Values

The general structure of the formulas below is seen repeatedly in probability theory. These calculations represent what are known as expected value calculations, and sometimes referred to as taking expectations. The general case is defined first, then specific examples are presented. 

Definition 7.35 Given a discrete random variable, $X : { \mathcal { S } }  \mathbb { R } \quad$ , and function $g ( x )$ defined on the range of X, $\mathbb { R } \mathrm { n g } [ X ] \subset \mathbb { R }$ , the expected value $o f g ( { \cal { X } } )$ , denoted $\operatorname { E } [ g ( X ) ]$ ， is defined as 

$$
\operatorname{E} [ g (X) ] = \sum_ {s _ {j} \in \mathcal {S}} g (X (s _ {j})) \operatorname * {P r} (s _ {j}).\tag{7.35}
$$

$I f \left\{ x _ { j } \right\} \subset \mathbb { R }$ denotes the range of X, and the p.d.f. of X is denoted by $f ( x )$ so that $f ( x _ { j } ) \equiv { \operatorname* { P r } } ( s _ { j } )$ with $x _ { j } \equiv { \cal X } ( s _ { j } )$ , then this expected value can be defined by 

$$
\operatorname{E} [ g (X) ] = \sum_ {j} g (x _ {j}) f (x _ {j}).\tag{7.36}
$$

In either case, this expectation is only defined when the associated summation is absolutely convergent, and so in the notation of (7.36), since $f ( x _ { j } ) \geq 0 .$ , it is required that 

$$
\sum_ {j} | g (x _ {j}) | f (x _ {j}) <   \infty .\tag{7.37}
$$

$H ( 7 . 3 7 )$ is not satisfied, we say that $\operatorname { E } [ g ( X ) ]$ does not exist. 

## Remark 7.36

1. The condition in (7.37) is automatically satisfied if the $\{ x _ { j } \}$ is finite. The purpose of this restriction in the countably infinite case is to avoid the problem discussed in section 6.1.4, that if only conditionally convergent, the value of this summation is not well defined and depends on the order in which the summation is carried out. 

2. All expectation formulas can be stated in terms of the random variable X, the sample space S, and its probability measure Pr, or directly in terms of the p.d.f. associated with X. In general, we will only provide the p.d.f. versions as in $( 7 . 3 6 )$ and leave it as an exercise for the reader to formulate the sample space versions as in (7.35). 

3. It is to be explicitly understood without further repetition that expectation definitions are valid only when the respective absolute convergence conditions as in (7.37) are satisfied. 

4. When neededfor clarity, a subscript is placed on the expectations symbol to identify what variable is involved in the expectation. For example, given p.d.f. $f ( x )$ , the meaning of $\operatorname { E } [ X ]$ is unambiguous, so expressing this as $\operatorname { E } _ { X } [ X ]$ is redundant. On the other hand, the meaning of E½XY is ambiguous, since it is not clear which variable is involved. So in this case one would clarify as $\operatorname { E } _ { X } [ X Y ] o r \operatorname { E } _ { Y } [ X Y ] o r \operatorname { E } _ { X Y } [ X Y ]$ 

Of course, all expectations of random variables in finite sample spaces exist when $g ( x )$ is defined and hence finitely valued on the range of X. However, for random variables on countably infinite sample spaces, expected values may not exist even when $g ( x )$ is defined on the range of X. 

Example 7.37 IfS is countally infinite, $X : S  \mathbb { N }$ is defined by $X ( s _ { j } ) = j$ with range equal to the positive integers, and $f ( j )$ is given by $\textstyle f ( j ) = { \frac { c } { i ^ { 2 } } }$ , where c is chosen so that $\textstyle \sum _ { j } f ( j ) = 1$ , then E½X does not exist, since $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname { E } [ X ] = \sum _ { j } j \frac { \stackrel { j } { c } } { j ^ { 2 } } = \sum _ { j } \frac { c } { j } } \end{array}$ is a multiple of the harmonic series and hence not finite. If instead X is defined by $\overset { \prime } { X } ( s _ { j } ) = ( - 1 ) \overset { j } { J } .$ , then again E½X does not exist. This is because, although E½X is conditionally convergent, it is not absolutely convergent. Similarly it is easy to find p.d.f.s with finite expected values up to some exponent: $g ( x ) = x ^ { n }$ , but with no finite expected values with larger exponents using power harmonic series from example 6.9 to define $f ( j )$ 

On the assumption that expected values exist, they are easy to work with in terms of addition and scalar multiplication. 

Proposition 7.38 $H g ( x )$ and $h ( x )$ are functions for which $\operatorname { E } [ g ( x ) ]$ and $\operatorname { E } [ h ( x ) ]$ exist, and $a , b ,$ c are real numbers, then $\operatorname { E } [ a g ( x ) + b h ( x ) + c ]$ exists and 

$$
\operatorname{E} [ a g (x) + b h (x) + c ] = a \operatorname{E} [ g (x) ] + b \operatorname{E} [ h (x) ] + c.\tag{7.38}
$$

Proof This result is immediate from the definition, but we must first verify that $a g ( x ) + b h ( x ) + c$ satisfies (7.37). This, of course, follows from the triangle inequality 

$$
\left| a g (x) + b h (x) + c \right| \leq | a | | g (x) | + | b | | h (x) | + | c |,
$$

and the assumption that $\operatorname { E } [ g ( x ) ]$ and $\operatorname { E } [ h ( x ) ]$ exist. 

On the other hand, expected values do not work well with multiplication and division, and as might be expected, 

$$
\operatorname{E} [ f (x) g (x) ] \neq \operatorname{E} [ f (x) ] \operatorname{E} [ g (x) ],
$$

$$
\operatorname{E} \left[ \frac {f (x)}{g (x)} \right] \neq \frac {\operatorname{E} [ f (x) ]}{\operatorname{E} [ g (x) ]}.
$$

## Conditional and Joint Expectations

Expected value calculations can also be defined with respect to joint probability density functions, as well as conditional probability density functions. For example, if $\overline { { \boldsymbol { X } } } = ( X _ { 1 } , X _ { 2 } )$ is a random vector with joint p.d.f. $f ( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } )$ , and $g ( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } )$ is defined on $\mathbb { R } \mathrm { n g } [ { \overline { { X } } } ] \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }$ , we define the joint expectation of $g ( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } )$ by 

$$
\operatorname{E} \left[ g \left(X _ {1}, X _ {2}\right) \right] = \sum_ {\left(x _ {1}, x _ {2}\right)} g \left(x _ {1}, x _ {2}\right) f \left(x _ {1}, x _ {2}\right).\tag{7.39}
$$

Many such calculations are possible with di¤ering values of $g ( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } )$ . One important application of this type of formula is in the case where $\{ X _ { j } \}$ are independent trials from a given p.d.f. Another important example is for the covariance of two random variables. Both are addressed below. 

If $f ( x _ { 1 } \mid x _ { 2 } )$ is one of the associated conditional p.d.f.s, and $g ( x )$ is given, then the conditional expected value or conditional expectation is defined as 

$$
\operatorname{E} \left[ g \left(X _ {1}\right) \mid X _ {2} = x _ {2} \right] = \sum_ {x _ {1}} g \left(x _ {1}\right) f \left(x _ {1} \mid x _ {2}\right).\tag{7.40}
$$

Sometimes for clarity, though cumbersome, the conditional expectation symbol is written with a subscript of $X _ { 1 } \mid X _ { 2 }$ as in $\operatorname { E } _ { X _ { 1 } \mid X _ { 2 } } [ g ( X _ { 1 } ) \mid X _ { 2 } ]$ or $\operatorname { E } [ g ( X _ { 1 } ) | X _ { 2 } ]$ 

Remark 7.39 Unlike most expected values, which provide numerical results, a conditional expectation can be interpreted as a function on the original sample space $s ,$ defined by $s \to \operatorname { E } [ g ( X _ { 1 } ) \mid X _ { 2 } ( s ) ]$ . It is in fact a random variable on $s ,$ since the preimage of an open interval $( a , b ) \subset \mathbb { R }$ is just the union of countably many events, which is an event in E. It is then the case that the expectation of this random variable under the $p . d . f . ~ f ( x _ { 2 } )$ equals the expectation of $\dot { \boldsymbol g } ( \boldsymbol x )$ using $f ( x _ { 1 } )$ . In other words, 

$$
\mathrm{E} _ {X _ {2}} \left[ \mathrm{E} _ {X _ {1} \mid X _ {2}} [ g (X _ {1}) \mid X _ {2} ] \right] = \mathrm{E} _ {X _ {1}} [ g (X _ {1}) ].\tag{7.41}
$$

The demonstration of this somewhat tediously notated formula is actually simple. $B y$ absolute convergence, we can reverse the order of the double summation and apply the law of total probability: 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathrm{E} _ {X _ {2}} [ \mathrm{E} _ {X _ {1} \mid X _ {2}} [ g (X _ {1}) \mid X _ {2} ] ] = \sum_ {x _ {2}} \left[ \sum_ {x _ {1}} g (x _ {1}) f (x _ {1} \mid x _ {2}) \right] f (x _ {2}) \\ = \sum_ {x _ {1}} g (x _ {1}) \left[ \sum_ {x _ {2}} f (x _ {1} \mid x _ {2}) f (x _ {2}) \right] \\ = \sum_ {x _ {1}} g (x _ {1}) f (x _ {1}). \end{array}
$$

This interpretation of $\operatorname { E } [ g ( X _ { 1 } ) | X _ { 2 } ]$ as a random variable on $\mathcal { S }$ is critical in advanced probability theory. 

Mean 

The mean of $X _ { z }$ , denoted $\mu ,$ is defined as $\mu = \operatorname { E } [ X ]$ 

$$
\mu = \sum_ {i} x _ {i} f (x _ {i}).\tag{7.42}
$$

In some applications, the random variable X may be defined in a complicated way, perhaps dependent on another random variable $Y ,$ and for which the conditional expectation, $\operatorname { E } [ X \mid Y ]$ is simpler to evaluate. An immediate application of (7.41) with $g ( X ) = X$ leads to the following identity between $\operatorname { E } [ X ]$ and the various conditional expectations $\operatorname { E } [ X \mid Y ]$ , which is known as the law of total expectation: 

$$
\operatorname{E} [ X ] = \operatorname{E} [ \operatorname{E} [ X \mid Y ] ].\tag{7.43}
$$

While this formula may at first appear ambiguous, a moment of reflection justifies that it is well defined even without the subscript clutter of (7.41). The inner expectation can only be defined relative to the conditional p.d.f. $f ( x | y )$ as $\operatorname { E } [ X \mid Y ] =$ $\textstyle \sum _ { i } x _ { i } f ( x _ { i } \mid Y )$ . Once this expectation is performed, the remaining term is a function of Y alone, and hence the outer expectation must be calculated relative to the marginal $\boldsymbol { \mathrm { p . d . f . , } } f ( y )$ . In other words, 

$$
\operatorname{E} [ \operatorname{E} [ X \mid Y ] ] = \sum_ {j} \sum_ {i} x _ {i} f (x _ {i} \mid y _ {j}) f (y _ {j}).
$$

## Variance

The variance of $X ,$ denoted $\sigma ^ { 2 }$ , is defined as $\operatorname { E } [ \left( X - \mu \right) ^ { 2 } ]$ 

$$
\sigma^ {2} = \sum_ {i} (x _ {i} - \mu) ^ {2} f (x _ {i}),\tag{7.44}
$$

and the standard deviation, denoted $\sigma ,$ is the positive square root of the variance. It is often more convenient to denote the variance by $\mathrm { V a r } [ X ]$ , and standard deviation by s.d.½X, as this notation has the advantage of making the random variable explicit. In addition one can also use the notation $\sigma _ { X } ^ { 2 }$ and $\sigma _ { X }$ 

It is often easier to calculate variance by first expanding $( x _ { i } - \mu ) ^ { 2 } = x _ { i } ^ { 2 } - 2 \mu x _ { i } +$ $\mu ^ { 2 }$ , and then using (7.38) to obtain 

$$
\sigma^ {2} = \operatorname{E} [ X ^ {2} ] - \operatorname{E} [ X ] ^ {2}.\tag{7.45}
$$

As noted above in the discussion of the mean, it may be the case that the random variable X is defined in a complicated way, perhaps dependent on another random variable Y, and that $\mathrm { V a r } [ X ]$ is di‰cult to estimate directly, yet the conditional variance $\operatorname { V a r } [ X \mid Y ]$ is simpler. Of course, this conditional variance is well defined as the variance of X, utilizing the conditional p.d.f. $f ( x \vert y )$ . In other words, 

$$
\operatorname{Var} [ X \mid Y ] = \sum_ {i} (x _ {i} - \mu_ {X \mid Y}) ^ {2} f (x _ {i} \mid Y),
$$

where the conditional mean is defined, $\mu _ { X \mid Y } = \operatorname { E } [ X \mid Y ]$ 

The question then becomes, can $\mathrm { V a r } [ X ]$ be recovered from the conditional variances $\operatorname { V a r } [ X \mid Y ]$ the same way that the mean can be recovered from the conditional means via (7.43)? The answer is ‘‘yes,’’ but with a slightly more complicated formula, known as the law of total variance: 

$$
\operatorname{Var} [ X ] = \operatorname{E} [ \operatorname{Var} [ X \mid Y ] ] + \operatorname{Var} [ \operatorname{E} [ X \mid Y ] ].\tag{7.46}
$$

Before addressing the derivation, note that the formula above is again well defined. As $\operatorname { V a r } [ X \mid Y ]$ and $\operatorname { E } [ X \mid Y ]$ are functions only of $Y , \operatorname { E } [ \operatorname { V a r } [ X \mid Y ] ]$ and $\operatorname { V a r } [ \operatorname { E } [ X \mid Y ] ]$ must be calculated using the marginal p.d.f. $f ( y )$ , and the variance term is defined as in (7.44), with $\mu = \operatorname { E } [ \operatorname { E } [ X \mid Y ] ] = \operatorname { E } [ X ]$ . Summarizing, we have 

$$
\operatorname{E} [ \operatorname{Var} [ X \mid Y ] ] = \sum_ {i} \operatorname{Var} [ X \mid y _ {i} ] f (y _ {i}),
$$

$$
\operatorname{Var} [ \mathrm{E} [ X \mid Y ] ] = \sum_ {i} (\mathrm{E} [ X \mid y _ {i} ] - \mu) ^ {2} f (y _ {i}).
$$

To derive $( 7 . 4 6 )$ , we use the variance formula in (7.45), and substitute the law of total expectation in (7.41): 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \operatorname{Var} [ X ] = \operatorname{E} [ X ^ {2} ] - (\operatorname{E} [ X ])) ^ {2} \\ = \operatorname{E} [ \operatorname{E} [ X ^ {2} \mid Y ] ] - (\operatorname{E} [ \operatorname{E} [ X \mid Y ] ]) ^ {2}. \end{array}
$$

Now another application of (7.45) is 

$$
\operatorname{E} [ X ^ {2} \mid Y ] = \operatorname{Var} [ X \mid Y ] + \operatorname{E} [ X \mid Y ] ^ {2},
$$

which is inserted into the formula above to produce: 

$$
\operatorname{Var} [ X ] = \operatorname{E} [ \operatorname{Var} [ X \mid Y ] ] + \operatorname{E} [ \operatorname{E} [ X \mid Y ] ^ {2} ] - (\operatorname{E} [ \operatorname{E} [ X \mid Y ] ]) ^ {2}.
$$

Finally, the last two terms are equal to $\operatorname { V a r } [ \operatorname { E } [ X \mid Y ] ]$ by another application of (7.45), completing the derivation. 

Because the laws of total probability, expectation, and variance are so important, the next proposition brings these results together: 

Proposition 7.40 Let X and Y be random variables on a discrete probability space S, with associated joint p.d.f. $f ( x , y )$ , marginal p.d.f.s $f ( x )$ and $f ( y )$ , and conditional p.d.f. $f ( x \vert y )$ . Then: 

1. Law oftotal probability, 

$$
f (x) = \sum_ {y} f (x \mid y) f (y).\tag{7.47}
$$

2. Law of total expectation, 

$$
\operatorname{E} [ X ] = \operatorname{E} [ \operatorname{E} [ X \mid Y ] ].\tag{7.48}
$$

3. Law of total variance, 

$$
\operatorname{Var} [ X ] = \operatorname{E} [ \operatorname{Var} [ X \mid Y ] ] + \operatorname{Var} [ \operatorname{E} [ X \mid Y ] ].\tag{7.49}
$$

Example 7.41 Let X denote the number of heads obtained in Y flips of a fair coin, where Y is the number of dots obtained in a roll of a fair die. The goal is to calculate $\operatorname { E } [ X ]$ and $\mathrm { V a r } [ X ]$ . To formalize a sample space, define S as the space ofn-flips ofa fair coin for $n = 1 , 2 , 3 , \ldots , 6 .$ So $\mathcal { S } = \{ ( F _ { 1 } , F _ { 2 } , \ldots , F _ { n } ) | 1 \leq n \leq 6 \}$ . Here $F _ { j } = 1$ for an H on the jth flip, and 0 otherwise, so S contains $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { n = 1 } ^ { 6 } 2 ^ { n } = 2 ^ { 7 } - 1 } \end{array}$ sample points. The probability measure is defined on each point by 

$$
\operatorname * {P r} \left[ \left(F _ {1}, F _ {2}, \dots , F _ {n}\right) \right] = \frac {1}{6} \frac {1}{2 ^ {n}}.
$$

Now X and Y are defined on S by 

$$
Y \left[ \left(F _ {1}, F _ {2}, \dots , F _ {n}\right) \right] = n,
$$

$$
X \left[ \left(F _ {1}, F _ {2}, \dots , F _ {n}\right) \right] = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} F _ {j},
$$

and so $\operatorname { R n g } [ Y ] = \left\{ 1 \leq n \leq 6 \right\}$ and $\operatorname { R n g } [ X ] = \{ 0 \leq m \leq 6 \}$ . Also $\begin{array} { r } { f ( n ) = \frac { 1 } { 6 } f o r } \end{array}$ all n. For $\operatorname { E } [ X \mid Y = n ]$ and $\operatorname { V a r } [ X \mid Y = n ]$ , we use formulas below in $( 7 . 9 9 )$ from section 7.6.2 on the binomial distribution. Then $\operatorname { E } [ X \mid Y = n ] = { \frac { n } { 2 } }$ , and from (7.48), $\operatorname { E } [ X ] = \operatorname { E } \left[ { \frac { n } { 2 } } \right]$ , so 

$$
\operatorname{E} [ X ] = \frac {1}{1 2} \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {6} n = \frac {2 1}{1 2}.
$$

Next, $\operatorname { V a r } [ X \mid Y = n ] = { \frac { n } { 4 } } , s o \operatorname { E } [ \operatorname { V a r } [ X \mid Y ] ] = { \frac { 2 1 } { 2 4 } }$ . Also from $\operatorname { E } [ X \mid Y = n ] = { \frac { n } { 2 } } ~ w e ~ o b -$ tain that 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \operatorname{Var} [ \mathrm{E} [ X \mid Y ] ] & = \mathrm{E} \left[ \frac {n ^ {2}}{4} \right] - \left(\mathrm{E} \left[ \frac {n}{2} \right]\right) ^ {2} \\ & = \frac {1}{2 4} \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {6} n ^ {2} - \left(\frac {2 1}{1 2}\right) ^ {2} \\ & = \frac {1 0 5}{1 4 4}. \end{array}
$$

Finally, using (7.49) obtains 

$$
\operatorname{Var} [ X ] = \frac {2 1}{2 4} + \frac {1 0 5}{1 4 4} = \frac {2 3 1}{1 4 4}.
$$

## Covariance and Correlation

As noted above, there are many expected values that can be defined with a joint p.d.f. One common set of expectations, given $f ( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } , \ldots , x _ { n } )$ , is to evaluate the covariance between any two of these random variables. With the associated marginal densities $f ( x _ { j } )$ , the respective means $\mu _ { j }$ and variances $\sigma _ { j } ^ { 2 }$ of each $X _ { j }$ can be calculated as discussed above. To calculate the covariance between $X _ { i }$ and $X _ { j }$ requires the joint p.d.f. $f ( x _ { i } , x _ { j } )$ . Although the notation is not standardized, we denote this expectation by $\sigma _ { i j }$ , and sometimes $\operatorname { C o v } ( X _ { i } , X _ { j } )$ , the covariance is defined by $\operatorname { E } [ ( X _ { i } - \mu _ { i } ) ( Y _ { j } - \mu _ { j } ) ]$ 

$$
\sigma_ {i j} = \sum_ {k, l} (x _ {k} - \mu_ {i}) (x _ {l} - \mu_ {j}) f (x _ {k}, x _ {l}).\tag{7.50}
$$

With a slight abuse of notation, we can define $\sigma _ { j j } \equiv \sigma _ { j } ^ { 2 } = \operatorname { V a r } [ X _ { j } ]$ 

Note that a calculation produces a result analogous to (7.45): 

$$
\sigma_ {i j} = \mathrm{E} [ X _ {i} Y _ {j} ] - \mathrm{E} [ X _ {i} ] \mathrm{E} [ Y _ {j} ].\tag{7.51}
$$

Also, if $X _ { i }$ and $X _ { j }$ are independent, then $f ( x _ { i } , x _ { j } ) = f ( x _ { i } ) f ( x _ { j } )$ , and it is apparent that $\sigma _ { i j } = 0$ , since 

$$
\sum_ {k l} \left(x _ {k} - \mu_ {i}\right) \left(x _ {l} - \mu_ {j}\right) f \left(x _ {k}, x _ {l}\right) = \sum_ {k} \left(x _ {k} - \mu_ {i}\right) f \left(x _ {k}\right) \sum_ {l} \left(x _ {l} - \mu_ {j}\right) f \left(x _ {l}\right).
$$

The correlation between $x _ { i }$ and $x _ { j } .$ denoted r , and sometimes $\rho _ { i j } .$ $\operatorname { C o r r } ( X _ { i } , X _ { j } )$ , is defined as 

$$
\rho_ {i j} = \frac {\sigma_ {i j}}{\sigma_ {i} \sigma_ {j}},\tag{7.52}
$$

which is equivalently calculated as $\begin{array} { r } { \rho _ { i j } = \sum _ { k , l } \left( \frac { x _ { k } - \mu _ { i } } { \sigma _ { i } } \right) \left( \frac { x _ { l } - \mu _ { j } } { \sigma _ { j } } \right) f ( x _ { k } , x _ { l } ) } \end{array}$ . The random variables are said to be uncorrelated if $\rho _ { i j } = 0$ , they are positively correlated if $\rho _ { i j } > 0 ;$ whereas they are said to be negatively correlated if $\rho _ { i j } < 0$ . As noted above, independent random variables are uncorrelated, and hence have $\rho _ { i j } = 0$ 

However, being uncorrelated is a weaker condition on two random variables than being independent. 

Example 7.42 Define $f ( x , y )$ by 

$$
f (x, y) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \frac {1}{3}, & (x, y) = (- 1, 1), \\ \frac {1}{3}, & (x, y) = (0, 0), \\ \frac {1}{3}, & (x, y) = (1, 1). \end{array} \right.
$$

Then $\begin{array} { r } { f ( x ) = \frac { 1 } { 3 } f o r \ x = - 1 , 0 , 1 } \end{array}$ , and $\begin{array} { r } { f ( y ) = { \frac { 2 } { 3 } } f o r \ y = 1 } \end{array}$ and $\begin{array} { r } { f ( y ) = \frac { 1 } { 3 } f o r \ y = 0 . } \end{array}$ . Consequently X and Y are not independent, since $f ( x , y ) \neq f ( x ) f ( y )$ . On the other hand, X and Y are uncorrelated, since $\operatorname { E } [ X Y ] = 0 , \operatorname { E } [ X ] = 0$ and $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname { E } [ Y ] = \frac { 2 } { 3 } } \end{array}$ imply that $\sigma _ { X Y } =$ $\operatorname { E } [ X Y ] - \operatorname { E } [ X ] \operatorname { E } [ Y ] = 0 .$ , and so $\rho _ { x y } = 0 .$ 

An important application of the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality is as follows: 

Proposition 7.43 Given random variables X, Y with joint p.d.f. $f ( x , y )$ 

$$
\left| \sigma_ {X Y} \right| \leq \sigma_ {X} \sigma_ {Y}.\tag{7.53}
$$

In other words, 

$$
- 1 \leq \rho_ {X Y} \leq 1.\tag{7.54}
$$

Proof Since $f ( x , y ) \geq 0$ , we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \sigma_ {X Y} = \sum_ {i, j} (x _ {i} - \mu_ {X}) (y _ {j} - \mu_ {Y}) f (x _ {i}, y _ {j}) \\ \qquad = \sum_ {i, j} \left[ (x _ {i} - \mu_ {X}) \sqrt {f (x _ {i} , y _ {j})} \right] \left[ (y _ {j} - \mu_ {Y}) \sqrt {f (x _ {i} , y _ {j})} \right]. \end{array}
$$

This second summation is seen to be an inner product, and by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, the square of this inner product is bounded by the product of the sums of squares: 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \sigma_ {X Y} ^ {2} \leq \sum_ {i, j} \Big [ (x _ {i} - \mu_ {X}) \sqrt {f (x _ {i} , y _ {j})} \Big ] ^ {2} \sum_ {i, j} \Big [ (y _ {j} - \mu_ {Y}) \sqrt {f (x _ {i} , y _ {j})} \Big ] ^ {2} \\ = \sum_ {i, j} (x _ {i} - \mu_ {X}) ^ {2} f (x _ {i}, y _ {j}) \sum_ {i, j} (y _ {j} - \mu_ {Y}) ^ {2} f (x _ {i}, y _ {j}) \\ = \sum_ {i} (x _ {i} - \mu_ {X}) ^ {2} f (x _ {i}) \sum_ {j} (y _ {j} - \mu_ {Y}) ^ {2} f (y _ {j}) = \sigma_ {X} ^ {2} \sigma_ {Y} ^ {2}. \end{array}
$$

The covariance also arises in the variance calculation of the sum of random variables, $\begin{array} { r } { X = \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } a _ { j } X _ { j } } \end{array}$ for constants $\{ a _ { j } \}$ . The associated p.d.f. used in the expected value calculation is the joint p.d.f., $f ( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } , \ldots , x _ { n } )$ . With this we see that 

$$
\mathrm{E} \left[ \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} a _ {j} X _ {j} \right] = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} a _ {j} \mathrm{E} [ X _ {j} ].\tag{7.55}
$$

Also 

$$
\begin{array}{c} (X - \operatorname{E} [ X ]) ^ {2} = \left(\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} a _ {j} [ X _ {j} - \operatorname{E} [ X _ {j} ] ]\right) ^ {2} \\ = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} a _ {i} a _ {j} [ X _ {i} - \operatorname{E} [ X _ {i} ] ] [ X _ {j} - \operatorname{E} [ X _ {j} ] ]. \end{array}
$$

After expectations are taken, this leads to 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \operatorname{Var} \left[ \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} a _ {j} X _ {j} \right] = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} a _ {i} a _ {j} \sigma_ {i j} \\ = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} a _ {j} ^ {2} \sigma_ {j} ^ {2} + 2 \sum_ {i <   j} a _ {i} a _ {j} \rho_ {i j} \sigma_ {i} \sigma_ {j}. \end{array}\tag{7.56a}
$$

ð7:56bÞ 

Note that when the component random variables are independent, or simply uncorrelated: 

$$
\operatorname{Var} \left[ \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} a _ {j} X _ {j} \right] = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} a _ {j} ^ {2} \sigma_ {j} ^ {2}.\tag{7.57}
$$

## General Moments

Generalizing the definition of the mean of a random variable, the nth moment, denoted $\mu _ { n } ^ { \prime } ,$ is defined as $\operatorname { E } [ X ^ { n } ]$ for $n \geq 0$ 

$$
\mu_ {n} ^ {\prime} = \sum_ {i} x _ {i} ^ {n} f (x _ {i}),\tag{7.58}
$$

so in particular, $\mu _ { 0 } ^ { \prime } = 1 , \mu _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } = \mu ,$ and $\mu _ { \gamma } ^ { \prime } = \sigma ^ { 2 } + \mu ^ { 2 }$ as noted in (7.45). 

Note that a direct application of (7.41) with $g ( X ) = X ^ { n }$ produces 

$$
\operatorname{E} [ X ^ {n} ] = \operatorname{E} [ \operatorname{E} [ X ^ {n} \mid Y ] ],
$$

as was used in the derivation of the law of total variance. 

## General Central Moments

Generalizing the definition of variance of a random variable, the nth central moment, denoted $\mu _ { n }$ , is defined as $\operatorname { E } [ ( X - \mu ) ^ { n } ]$ for $n \geq 0$ 

$$
\mu_ {n} = \sum_ {i} (x _ {i} - \mu) ^ {n} f (x _ {i}),\tag{7.59}
$$

so in particular, $\mu _ { 0 } = 1 , \mu _ { 1 } = 0$ , and $\mu _ { 2 } = \sigma ^ { 2 }$ 

## Absolute Moments

When n is odd, the value of the moments $\operatorname { E } [ X ^ { n } ]$ and/or $\operatorname { E } [ ( X - \mu ) ^ { n } ]$ can reflect the cancellation of positive and negative terms. The notion of absolute moments is used to value the associated absolutely convergent series. The nth absolute moment, denoted $\mu _ { | n | } ^ { \prime } ,$ is defined as $\operatorname { E } [ | X | ^ { n } ]$ for $n \geq 0$ 

$$
\mu_ {| n |} ^ {\prime} = \sum_ {i} | x _ {i} | ^ {n} f (x _ {i}),\tag{7.60}
$$

and the nth absolute central moment, denoted $\mu _ { | n | }$ , is defined as $\operatorname { E } [ | X - \mu | ^ { n } ]$ for $n \geq 0 !$ 

$$
\mu_ {| n |} = \sum_ {i} \left| x _ {i} - \mu \right| ^ {n} f (x _ {i}).\tag{7.61}
$$

This notation is descriptive but not standard. 

Because of the condition in (7.37), absolute moments always exist when the corresponding moments exist. Of course, for n even, the absolute moments agree with the respective moments defined above. For n odd, the moments may agree with the absolute moments, for instance, if the range of X is positive, but the central moments and absolute central moments will not agree, since $\{ x _ { i } - \mu \}$ will always have both positive and negative terms. 

## Moment-Generating Function

The moment-generating function (m.g.f.), as the name implies, reflects an expected value calculation that produces a function rather than a numerical constant. Denoted $M ( t )$ , or $M _ { X } ( t )$ , it is defined as $\operatorname { E } [ e ^ { X t } ]$ 

$$
M _ {X} (t) = \sum_ {i} e ^ {x _ {i} t} f (x _ {i}).\tag{7.62}
$$

Of course, $M _ { X } ( 0 ) = 1$ , so the question of existence of the m.g.f. relates to existence for some interval, $| t | < T$ . It is important to note at the outset that $M ( t )$ does not always exist. 

As we have seen before and will prove in chapter 9, the exponential function can be expanded into the power series: 

$$
e ^ {x} = \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {x ^ {n}}{n !}.\tag{7.63}
$$

This series converges absolutely for all x by the ratio test, 

$$
\left| \frac {\frac {x ^ {n + 1}}{(n + 1) !}}{\frac {x ^ {n}}{n !}} \right| = \left| \frac {x}{n + 1} \right|\rightarrow 0 \quad \text { as } n \rightarrow \infty ;
$$

so what needs to be shown in chapter 9 is that the function of x defined by this series is indeed equal to $e ^ { x }$ . 

Substituting the corresponding expression for $e ^ { x _ { i } t }$ into (7.62), and using the arithmetic properties of expected value noted above and the assumption of absolute convergence justified by the existence of $M _ { X } ( t )$ , we derive 

$$
M _ {X} (t) = \sum_ {i} \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {(x _ {i} t) ^ {n}}{n !} f (x _ {i}) = \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {t ^ {n}}{n !} \sum_ {i} x _ {i} ^ {n} f (x _ {i}),
$$

and hence 

$$
M _ {X} (t) = \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {\mu_ {n} ^ {\prime} t ^ {n}}{n !}.\tag{7.64}
$$

Of course, since all terms in the summation are positive, all these manipulations require the assumption that $M _ { X } ( t )$ actually exists and so the series in (7.62) converges and hence converges absolutely. This is always the case for finite sample spaces, but not necessarily the case when the sample space is countably infinite. As seen in section 6.1.4, it is the absolute convergence of this series that justifies the manipulations in the double series and the reversal of the order of the summations. 

In chapter 9 we will see that the moments $\{ \mu _ { n } ^ { \prime } \}$ can in turn be recovered from the moment-generating function, or better said, ‘‘generated’’ from the m.g.f., if it converges in an interval containing 0. Specifically, with $M _ { X } ^ { ( n ) } ( t )$ denoting the nth derivative of the function $M _ { X } ( t )$ with respect to $t ,$ we will see that 

$$
\mu_ {n} ^ {\prime} = M _ {X} ^ {(n)} (0).\tag{7.65}
$$

A simple modification to the definition of the m.g.f. can be introduced that will generate the central moments. Specifically, since $X - \mu$ has the same p.d.f. as does $X ,$ , its moment-generating function is defined by $\begin{array} { r } { M _ { X - \mu } ( t ) = \sum _ { i } e ^ { ( x _ { i } - \mu ) t } f ( x _ { i } ) } \end{array}$ . Applying (7.63) obtains 

$$
M _ {X - \mu} (t) = \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {\mu_ {n} t ^ {n}}{n !},\tag{7.66}
$$

from which is produced 

$$
\mu_ {n} = M _ {X - \mu} ^ {(n)} (0).\tag{7.67}
$$

For a joint probability density function, $f ( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } , \ldots , x _ { n } )$ , the moment-generating function is analogously defined. The definition above where $M _ { X } ( t ) \equiv \operatorname { E } [ e ^ { X t } ]$ is generalized so that the m.g.f. is now a function of $\left( t _ { 1 } , t _ { 2 } , \ldots , t _ { n } \right)$ , and defined with the aid of boldface vector notation as $M _ { \mathrm { X } } ( { \bf t } ) \equiv \mathrm { E } [ e ^ { { \bf X } \cdot { \bf t } } ]$ , where X t denotes the inner product. In other words, 

$$
M _ {\mathbf {X}} (\mathbf {t}) = \sum_ {(x _ {1}, x _ {2}, \dots , x _ {n})} e ^ {\sum x _ {i} t _ {i}} f (x _ {1}, x _ {2}, \dots , x _ {n}).\tag{7.68}
$$

If the random variables in the definition of $f ( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } , \ldots , x _ { n } )$ are independent, then (7.34) is satisfied, so 

$$
M _ {\mathbf {X}} (\mathbf {t}) = \prod_ {i = 1} ^ {n} M _ {X _ {i}} (t _ {i}).
$$

If the random variables are independent and identically distributed, then with $Y =$ $\textstyle \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } X _ { i }$ we derive from (7.34) and directly from $M _ { Y } ( t ) \dot { = } \operatorname { E } \left[ e ^ { t \sum X _ { i } } \right]$ that 

$$
M _ {Y} (t) = \left[ M _ {X} (t) \right] ^ {n}.\tag{7.69}
$$

## Characteristic Function

The characteristic function (c.f.) is defined similarly to the m.g.f., and it will again be possible to generate moments from it, but it has the advantage that it always exists. The disadvantage to some is that while $M _ { X } ( t )$ is a function $M _ { X } ( t ) : \mathbb { R } \overset { } { \longrightarrow } \mathbb { R }$ , the characteristic function, denoted $C _ { X } ( t )$ , is a function $C _ { X } ( t ) : \mathbb { R } \overset { } { \longrightarrow } \mathbb { C }$ . Specifically, $C _ { X } ( t ) = \mathbb { E } [ e ^ { i X t } ]$ , where i denotes the ‘‘imaginary unit $\mathbf { \bar { \rho } } _ { i } = \mathbf { \sqrt { - 1 } }$ , producing 

$$
C _ {X} (t) = \sum_ {j} e ^ {i x _ {j} t} f (x _ {j}).\tag{7.70}
$$

It is straightforward to confirm that $C _ { X } ( t )$ exists for all $t \in \mathbb { R } .$ , since the summation converges absolutely. This is demonstrated using the triangle inequality and a consequence of Euler’s formula: that $\vert e ^ { i x _ { j } t } \vert = 1$ for all t and x<sub>j</sub>. Specifically, 

$$
\left| C _ {X} (t) \right| \leq \sum_ {j} \left| e ^ {i x _ {j} t} f \left(x _ {j}\right) \right| = \sum_ {j} f \left(x _ {j}\right) = 1.
$$

Unlike the case of the m.g.f., which may not exist but is di¤erentiable when it does exist, the characteristic function always exists, but it need not be di¤erentiable. However, if all moments exist, then using the same manipulations above, justified by absolute converge, produces 

$$
C _ {X} (t) = \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {\mu_ {n} ^ {\prime} (i t) ^ {n}}{n !},\tag{7.71}
$$

and once again the moments can be recovered from this function as in (7.65). With analogous notation, 

$$
\mu_ {n} ^ {\prime} = \frac {1}{i ^ {n}} C _ {X} ^ {(n)} (0).\tag{7.72}
$$

Central moments can again be generated if they exist using $C _ { X - \mu } ( t ) =$ $\textstyle \sum _ { j } e ^ { i ( x _ { j } - \mu ) t } f ( x _ { j } )$ ; then 

$$
C _ {X - \mu} (t) = \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {\mu_ {n} (i t) ^ {n}}{n !},\tag{7.73}
$$

$$
\mu_ {n} = \frac {1}{i ^ {n}} C _ {X - \mu} ^ {(n)} (0).\tag{7.74}
$$

For a joint probability density function $f ( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } , \ldots , x _ { n } )$ , the characteristic function is analogously defined. The definition above where $C _ { X } ( t ) = \mathbb { E } [ e ^ { i X t } ]$ is generalized so that the c.f. is a function of $\left( t _ { 1 } , t _ { 2 } , \ldots , t _ { n } \right)$ , and defined with the aid of boldface vector notation as $C _ { \mathbf { X } } ( \mathbf { t } ) \equiv \mathrm { E } [ e ^ { i \mathbf { X } \cdot \mathbf { t } } ]$ . In other words, 

$$
C _ {\mathbf {X}} (\mathbf {t}) = \sum_ {(x _ {1}, x _ {2}, \dots , x _ {n})} e ^ {i \sum x _ {j} t _ {j}} f (x _ {1}, x _ {2}, \dots , x _ {n}).\tag{7.75}
$$

Remark 7.44 An important property of the moment-generating and characteristic functions is that they ‘‘characterize’’ the discrete probability density function (a property we will prove in chapter 8 but only in the case offinite discrete random variables). The proof in the more general cases requires the tools of real analysis and complex analysis. What ‘‘characterize’’ means is that if $C _ { X } ( t ) = C _ { Y } ( t )$ or $M _ { X } ( t ) = M _ { Y } ( t )$ for random variables X and Y, and for $t \in I$ where I is any open interval containing 0, then the discrete probability density functions are equal: $f ( x ) = g ( y )$ . In the finite discrete case this means that if $\{ x _ { i } \} _ { i = 1 } ^ { n }$ and $\{ y _ { j } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { m }$ are the respective domains of these probability functions, arranged in increasing order, then $n = m , x _ { i } = y _ { i }$ and $f ( x _ { i } ) = g ( y _ { i } )$ for all i. The m.g.f. and $c . f .$ also characterize the p.d.f. of random variables in the more general cases to be developed later. Since the characteristic function always exists, this result can be applied to any p.d.f. and in any context. 

## *7.5.2 Moments of Sample Data

An important application of the general random vector expectation formula (7.39) is to so-called sample data expectations. In this section we provide a theoretical framework for the sample statistics introduced in section 3.3.2. 

Given a sample space $s ,$ we have the theoretical framework for a random sample or independent trials introduced in section 7.2.6 above. Specifically, recall that a random sample of size n was identified with a sample point in a new n-trial sample space, denoted ${ \mathcal { S } } ^ { n }$ , that was given a probability structure defined in (7.7). In this section we apply this structure to random samples of a given random variable, and derive some important formulas related to the moments of these samples. 

In the space S we assume that there is given a random variable X, and define a random vector ${ \overline { { X } } } = ( X _ { 1 } , X _ { 2 } , \ldots , X _ { n } )$ on ${ \mathcal { S } } ^ { n }$ . For $\bar { s } = ( s _ { 1 } , s _ { 2 } , \ldots , s _ { n } ) \in \mathcal { S } ^ { n }$ , we define 

$X _ { j } ( \bar { s } ) = X ( s _ { j } )$ . In the same way that $\left( s _ { 1 } , s _ { 2 } , \ldots , s _ { n } \right)$ represents a random sample of n possible sample points, with probability in ${ \mathcal { S } } ^ { n }$ defined so that $\begin{array} { r } { P _ { n } ( \bar { s } ) = \prod _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } \operatorname* { P r } ( s _ { j } ) } \end{array}$ the random vector of values, $\overline { { \cal X } } ( \bar { s } ) = ( X _ { 1 } ( \bar { s } ) , X _ { 2 } ( \bar { s } ) , \ldots , X _ { n } ( \bar { s } ) ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ is a random sample of the values assumed by X on S. In other words, the components of this random vector are independent in the formal meaning given in (7.34) above. 

To see this, let $f ( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } , \ldots , x _ { n } )$ be the joint p.d.f. defined on the $\mathrm { R n g } [ \overline { { X } } ]$ . That is, 

$$
f (x _ {1}, x _ {2}, \ldots , x _ {n}) = P _ {n} (X _ {1} ^ {- 1} (x _ {1}), X _ {2} ^ {- 1} (x _ {2}), \ldots , X _ {n} ^ {- 1} (x _ {n})).
$$

Then by (7.7), 

$$
f (x _ {1}, x _ {2}, \dots , x _ {n}) = \prod_ {j = 1} ^ {n} \operatorname * {P r} (X _ {j} ^ {- 1} (x _ {j}))
$$

$$
= \prod_ {j = 1} ^ {n} f (x _ {j}),
$$

where $f ( x )$ is the p.d.f. of the random variable $X .$ 

In summary, we see that if a random variable X on $\mathcal { S }$ is generalized as above to a random vector $\bar { X }$ on the n-trial sample space ${ \mathcal { S } } ^ { n }$ , then the collection of component random variables $\{ X _ { j } ( \bar { s } ) \}$ comprises independent random variables on $\mathcal { S }$ in the sense defined above, and 

$$
f (x _ {1}, x _ {2}, \dots , x _ {n}) = \prod_ {j = 1} ^ {n} f (x _ {j}).\tag{7.76}
$$

Initially this construction of a random sample may appear overly formal and unnecessary. In applications the random variable X is usually defined as the outcome of an experiment, or as an observation, and the notion of independent trials is understood as meaning that the experiment is repeated many times, or other observations are made. In such cases the truth of the identity in (7.76) would appear obvious to anyone that has flipped a coin, or rolled dice, and so forth. And in many applications this is a perfectly legitimate intuitive framework for what a random sample is, and perfectly legitimate justification for the meaning of independent sample. 

But intuition does not always guarantee that a rigorous development is possible. So the construction above provides a rigorous construction, in a discrete sample space context, of what a random sample from a sample space represents, and also, what n independent trials of a random variable means. And better than our intuition, this formality will lead the way to the corresponding ideas in the less intuitive frameworks. 

## Definition 7.45

1. Given a discrete sample space S and a random variable $X : S  \mathbb { R }$ , the terminology that $\{ X _ { j } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { n }$ are n-independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) random variables will mean that ${ \overline { { X } } } \equiv ( X _ { 1 } , X _ { 2 } , \ldots , X _ { n } )$ is a random vector on ${ \mathcal { S } } ^ { n }$ , where for $\bar { s } = ( s _ { 1 } , s _ { 2 } , \ldots , s _ { n } )$ $\in S ^ { n }$ the component random variables are defined by $X _ { j } ( \bar { s } ) = X ( s _ { j } )$ . In other words, the collection $\{ X _ { j } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { n }$ consists of independent random variables in that the joint $p . d . f .$ $f ( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } , \ldots , x _ { n } )$ , satisfies $( 7 . 7 6 )$ , and each component random variable has the same probability densityfunction as X. When $n = \infty$ , the terminology that $\{ X _ { j } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { \infty }$ are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) random variables means that this is true of $\{ X _ { j } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { n }$ for any n. 

2. The terminology that $\{ x _ { j } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { n }$ is a random sample from X ofsize n means that there is an $\bar { s } = ( s _ { 1 } , s _ { 2 } , \ldots , s _ { n } ) \in \mathcal { S } ^ { n }$ , selected according to the probability measure $P _ { n }$ on ${ \mathcal { S } } ^ { n }$ so that $( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } , \ldots , x _ { n } ) = ( X ( s _ { 1 } ) , X ( s _ { 2 } ) , \ldots , X ( s _ { n } ) )$ . In practice, this sample can be generated iteratively byfirst selecting independent $\left\{ s _ { j } \right\} _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } \subset { \mathcal { S } }$ (see section $7 . 7$ on generating random samples), and defining $\left( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } , \ldots , x _ { n } \right)$ as above. 

Remark 7.46 It is standard notation in probability theory that a capital letter is used for the a random variable, such as $X ,$ while a lowercase letter, such as $x ,$ is used to represent a realization, or sample point, of the random variable selected according to the probabilities implied by the probability density function of X. Also note that the equivalence of the approaches to a random sample in 2 of definition 7.45 above is due to the probability measure $P _ { n }$ satisfying (7.7). 

## Sample Mean

If $\{ X _ { j } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { n }$ are n independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) random variables on $s ,$ , the sample mean, denoted ${ \hat { X } } _ { ; }$ , is a random variable ${ \hat { X } } : S ^ { n }  \mathbb { R }$ defined by 

$$
\hat {X} \equiv \frac {1}{n} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} X _ {j},\tag{7.77}
$$

with probability density function given by $\begin{array} { r } { f ( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } , \ldots , x _ { n } ) = \prod _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } f ( x _ { j } ) } \end{array}$ , where $f ( x )$ is the p.d.f. of X. 

When a specific sample is drawn or observed, that is, when $\{ X _ { j } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } = \{ x _ { j } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { n }$ , the application of (7.77) to these data yields the numerical value denoted $\hat { \mu }$ or m in section 3.3.2. 

The distinction here is the explicit recognition that any such observation $\left\{ x _ { j } \right\} _ { j = 1 } ^ { n }$ is simply based on one sample point in the sample space ${ \mathcal { S } } ^ { n }$ , and that in more general terms, the calculation produces not a single and unique numerical value but only one of many possible values that the random variable $\hat { X }$ assumes on this sample space. Considered as a random variable, it is natural to inquire into its moments, as we do next. 

Mean of the Sample Mean By definition, we have that 

$$
\operatorname{E} [ \hat {X} ] = \sum_ {(x _ {1}, x _ {2}, \dots , x _ {n})} \left(\frac {1}{n} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} x _ {j}\right) f (x _ {1}, x _ {2}, \dots , x _ {n}).
$$

This formula simplifies using (7.76) and the observation that for any $x _ { j }$ , 

$$
\sum_ {(x _ {1}, x _ {2}, \dots , x _ {n})} x _ {j} \prod_ {k = 1} ^ {n} f (x _ {k}) = \sum_ {x _ {j}} x _ {j} f (x _ {j}) = \operatorname{E} [ X ],
$$

since $\textstyle \sum _ { x _ { k } } f ( x _ { k } ) = 1$ for $k \neq j$ . Combining, we get that 

$$
\operatorname{E} [ \hat {X} ] = \operatorname{E} [ X ],\tag{7.78}
$$

provided that $\operatorname { E } [ X ]$ exists. In other words, the expected value of the sample mean is the expected value of the original random variable $X .$ 

Variance of the Sample Mean Denoting $\operatorname { E } [ X ]$ by $\mu ,$ we have that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \operatorname{Var} [ \hat {X} ] = \operatorname{E} [ (\hat {X} - \mu) ^ {2} ] \\ = \sum_ {(x _ {1}, x _ {2}, \dots , x _ {n})} \left(\frac {1}{n} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} (x _ {j} - \mu)\right) ^ {2} f (x _ {1}, x _ {2}, \dots , x _ {n}). \end{array}
$$

Again using (7.76), we get 

$$
\operatorname{Var} [ \hat {X} ] = \frac {1}{n ^ {2}} \left[ \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} (x _ {j} - \mu) ^ {2} f (x _ {j}) \right] = \frac {\sigma^ {2}}{n}.
$$

This result is due to the fact that the mixed terms such as $( x _ { j } - \mu ) ( x _ { k } - \mu ) f ( x _ { j } ) f ( x _ { k } )$ with $j \neq k$ , have expectation of $0 ,$ since the summations can be done sequentially. 

Summarizing, we get 

$$
\mathrm{Var} [ \hat {X} ] = \frac {\sigma_ {X} ^ {2}}{n},\tag{7.79}
$$

provided that $\sigma _ { X } ^ { 2 }$ exists, and correspondingly 

$$
\text { s.d. } [ \hat {X} ] = \frac {\sigma_ {X}}{\sqrt {n}}.\tag{7.80}
$$

m.g.f. of Sample Mean Noting that $\begin{array} { r } { e ^ { t \hat { X } } = \prod _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } e ^ { t X _ { j } / n } } \end{array}$ , and applying the same method as above, we get that 

$$
M _ {\hat {X}} (t) = \left[ M _ {X} \left(\frac {t}{n}\right) \right] ^ {n},\tag{7.81}
$$

provided that $M _ { X } { \left( { \textstyle { \frac { t } { n } } } \right) }$ exists. 

## Sample Variance

If $\{ X _ { j } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { n }$ are n independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) random variables on $s ,$ , the unbiased sample variance is defined as 

$$
\hat {V} = \frac {1}{n - 1} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} (X _ {j} - \hat {X}) ^ {2},\tag{7.82}
$$

where $\begin{array} { r } { \hat { X } = \frac { 1 } { n } \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } X _ { j } } \end{array}$ $\hat { V }$ is again a random variable $\hat { V } : { \cal S } ^ { n } \to \mathbb { R }$ with a probability density function given by $\begin{array} { r } { f ( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } , \ldots , x _ { n } ) = \prod _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } f ( x _ { j } ) } \end{array}$ , where $f ( x )$ is the p.d.f. of $X$ . Note that the sample variance is defined with the sample mean ${ \hat { X } } ,$ , and not the theoretical mean $\mu .$ As we will see, this is the reason that it is necessary to use $\scriptstyle { \frac { 1 } { n - 1 } }$ in the formula above rather than the more natural value of $\textstyle { \frac { \cdot { \mathrm { ~ \textstyle ~ 1 ~ } } } { n } }$ . 

As was the case for the sample mean $\hat { X }$ , when a specific sample is drawn or observed—that is, when $\{ X _ { j } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } = \{ x _ { j } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { n }$ —the application of (7.82) to these data yields the numerical value denoted $\hat { \sigma } ^ { 2 }$ or $s ^ { 2 }$ in section 3.3.2, there defined with $n - 1$ rather than n. However, once again the perspective here is that any such observation $\{ x _ { j } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { n }$ is simply one sample point in the sample space ${ \mathcal { S } } ^ { n }$ , and that in more general terms, the calculation produces not a single and unique numerical value but only one of many possible values that the random variable $\hat { V }$ assumes on this sample space. Considered as a random variable, it is natural to inquire into its moments, as we do next. 

Mean of Sample Variance The calculation of $\operatorname { E } [ \hat { V } ]$ is complicated by the fact that the random variables appear in two places in the squared terms, explicitly in the $X _ { j }$ terms, and implicitly in the $\hat { X }$ term. A simple trick is to write $X _ { j } - { \hat { X } } = ( X _ { j } - \mu ) -$ $( { \hat { X } } - \mu )$ and $\begin{array} { r } { \hat { X } - \mu = \frac { 1 } { n } \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { n } ( X _ { k } - \mu ) } \end{array}$ , from which we get 

$$
\left(X _ {j} - \hat {X}\right) ^ {2} = \left(X _ {j} - \mu\right) ^ {2} - 2 \left(X _ {j} - \mu\right) (\hat {X} - \mu) + \left(\hat {X} - \mu\right) ^ {2}
$$

$$
= (X _ {j} - \mu) ^ {2} - \frac {2}{n} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} [ (X _ {j} - \mu) (X _ {k} - \mu) ] + \frac {1}{n ^ {2}} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} [ (X _ {i} - \mu) (X _ {k} - \mu) ].
$$

Summed over $j ,$ the second and third term then combine, producing 

$$
\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} (X _ {j} - \hat {X}) ^ {2} = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} (X _ {j} - \mu) ^ {2} - \frac {1}{n} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} [ (X _ {i} - \mu) (X _ {k} - \mu) ].
$$

Assuming that $\sigma ^ { 2 }$ exists, and taking expectations, we get 

$$
\operatorname{E} \left[ \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} (X _ {j} - \hat {X}) ^ {2} \right] = (n - 1) \sigma^ {2},
$$

since the expectation of mixed terms in the double sum, when $i \neq k$ , is 0 because of independence. This identity is equivalent to 

$$
\operatorname{E} [ \hat {V} ] = \sigma^ {2}.\tag{7.83}
$$

It is this identity that motivates the use of the term ‘‘unbiased’’ for the sample variance formula given above. It is unbiased in the sense that the expected value of this statistic is the theoretical value of what is being estimated. In that sense, from (7.78) it is also the case that $\hat { X }$ is an unbiased estimator of the theoretical mean $\mu \equiv \operatorname { E } [ X ]$ but this formula is never called the unbiased sample mean. 

It is easy to check that if the theoretical mean, $\mu ,$ is known and the sample variance defined as in (7.82) but with $\mu$ rather than ${ \hat { X } } ,$ , then the correct coe‰cient in (7.82) would be $\textstyle { \frac { 1 } { n } }$ , in that with this coe‰cient (7.83) would again be derived. But in most applications this is not relevant since sampling implies limited knowledge of the theoretical distribution and its theoretical moments, so it may be illogical to assume that $\mu$ is known. 

Remark 7.47 As it turns out, there is another calculation of sample variance that uses $\frac { 1 } { n }$ in its formulation rather than $\scriptstyle { \frac { 1 } { n - 1 } }$ , and yet also uses ${ \hat { X } } .$ . This particular formulation is known as the maximum likelihood estimator of the sample variance, and since the notation is not standardized, we use 

$$
\hat {\sigma} _ {M L E} ^ {2} = \frac {1}{n} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} (x _ {j} - \hat {X}) ^ {2},\tag{7.84}
$$

where $\begin{array} { r } { \hat { X } = \frac { 1 } { n } \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } x _ { j } } \end{array}$ . By the analysis above, if this version of a sample variance is defined as a random variable on ${ \mathcal { S } } ^ { n }$ analogously to $\hat { V } ,$ it is biased on the small side, in that 

$$
\mathrm{E} [ \hat {\sigma} _ {M L E} ^ {2} ] = \frac {n - 1}{n} \sigma^ {2}.\tag{7.85}
$$

The idea behind the MLE calculation is way ahead of our mathematical development, but it can be presented in an intuitive way. Assume that a sample has been drawn or observed, $\left\{ x _ { j } \right\} _ { j = 1 } ^ { n }$ , andfor various reasons we believe a particular form for the p.d.f. of the observed random variable, $f ( x )$ . In this case as in many, the assumed p.d.f. is that of the normal distribution, which is formally introduced in chapter 8 and studied in chapter 10. This distribution will be seen to be characterized by only two moments, m and $\sigma ^ { 2 } .$ . The question is then, given this assumed distribution, what estimates for m and $\sigma ^ { 2 }$ will maximize the probability of the observed sample? In other words, What estimates for m and $\sigma ^ { 2 }$ will maximize the likelihood of observing the given sample? 

Since the sample p.d.f. is $\begin{array} { r } { f ( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } , \ldots , x _ { n } ) = \prod _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } f ( x _ { j } ) } \end{array}$ , as seen in (7.76), and $f ( x )$ only depends on m and $\sigma ^ { 2 }$ , this question reduces to determining the values of these parameters that maximize $\textstyle \prod _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } f ( x _ { j } )$ , the probability of the sample point $( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } , \ldots ,$ $x _ { n } )$ under this distributional assumption. This function to be maximized is actually a function of the parameters $\mu$ and $\sigma ^ { 2 } { } _ { ; }$ , since the sample point $\left( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } , \ldots , x _ { n } \right)$ is fixed and known. Determining the maximum value ofa function is an application ofcalculus and will be seen in chapter 9 for one variable functions, while this particular application with two variables requires multivariate calculus. As it turns out, the MLE estimators for m and $\sigma ^ { 2 }$ are $\hat { X }$ and ${ \hat { \sigma } } _ { M L E } ^ { 2 } .$ 

Variance of Sample Variance Because of (7.83) the needed calculation is that of $\operatorname { V a r } [ { \hat { V } } ] = \operatorname { E } [ ( { \hat { \sigma } } ^ { 2 } - \sigma ^ { 2 } ) ^ { 2 } ]$ , which involves some messy algebra and some determination on the part of the analyst. To make this calculation reasonably tractable, we use the approach in (7.45) that variance equals the second moment less the mean squared, which becomes $\mathrm { V a r } [ \hat { V } ] = \mathrm { E } [ \hat { V } ^ { 2 } ] - \bar { ( } \mathrm { E } [ \hat { V } ] ) ^ { 2 } = \mathrm { E } [ \hat { V } ^ { 2 } ] - \sigma ^ { 4 }$ . From the algebra in the derivation of the mean of the sample variance, recall that 

$$
(n - 1) \hat {V} = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} (X _ {j} - \hat {X}) ^ {2} = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} Y _ {j} ^ {2} - \frac {1}{n} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} Y _ {i} Y _ {k},
$$

where we simplify notation with $Y _ { j } = X _ { j } - \mu .$ . The key is that $\operatorname { E } [ Y _ { j } ] = 0 _ { \mathrm { ; } }$ , and so in any expression in which there is at least one $Y _ { j }$ term to the first power, the expectation will be zero and can be ignored. 

This expression squared, which equals $( n - 1 ) ^ { 2 } { \hat { V } } ^ { 2 }$ , is then 

$$
\left[ \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} (X _ {j} - \hat {X}) ^ {2} \right] ^ {2} = \left[ \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} Y _ {j} ^ {2} \right] ^ {2} - \frac {2}{n} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} Y _ {j} ^ {2} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} Y _ {i} Y _ {k} + \frac {1}{n ^ {2}} \left[ \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} Y _ {i} Y _ {k} \right] ^ {2}.
$$

While initially ominous looking, we are only interested in determining how many terms of each ‘‘type’’ there are. For example, the squared first expression produces a sum of $Y _ { j } ^ { 2 } Y _ { k } ^ { 2 }$ terms, which fall into two types: one if $j = k$ and another if $j \neq k$ . Any term of the first type has expectation $\mu _ { 4 }$ , the fourth central moment of $X ,$ and any of the second type have expectation $\mu _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } = \sigma ^ { 4 }$ 

Using the combinatorics discussed earlier, we have n terms of the first type and $n ( n - 1 )$ of the second, since every $j$ can be paired with $( n - 1 ) – k \mathrm { s }$ . Hence the first expression becomes 

$$
\mathrm{E} \left[ \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} Y _ {j} ^ {2} \right] ^ {2} = n \mu_ {4} + n (n - 1) \sigma^ {4}.
$$

The second expression produces four types of terms: 

$$
Y _ {j} ^ {4}, \quad Y _ {j} ^ {3} Y _ {i}, \quad Y _ {j} ^ {2} Y _ {k} ^ {2}, \quad Y _ {j} ^ {2} Y _ {i} Y _ {k},
$$

where the subscripts are meant to di¤er. These terms have expectations of $\mu _ { 4 } , 0 , \sigma ^ { 4 }$ and 0, respectively, since $\operatorname { E } [ Y _ { k } ] = 0$ . The challenge is then counting the types, and all we are concerned with is the first and third type. Again, we draw on combinatorics and determine that there are n of the first type and $n ( n - 1 )$ of the third. Combined, the second expression becomes 

$$
\mathrm{E} \left[ - \frac {2}{n} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} Y _ {j} ^ {2} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} Y _ {i} Y _ {k} \right] = - 2 \mu_ {4} - 2 (n - 1) \sigma^ {4}.
$$

The third expression produces five di¤erent types of terms, the four above and $Y _ { i } Y _ { j } Y _ { k } Y _ { l }$ . Of these five, we only need to evaluate the first and third, since all others have expectation of 0. Again, there are n of the first type, but for the third, the combinatorics for this expression are di¤erent. First o¤, $\begin{array} { r } { \left[ \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { \bar { n } } \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { n } Y _ { i } Y _ { k } \right] ^ { 2 } = \left[ \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } Y _ { i } \right] ^ { 4 } } \end{array}$ , and from the multinomial formula in (7.19), the coe‰cient of every $Y _ { j } ^ { 2 } Y _ { k } ^ { 2 }$ term is $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { 4 ! } { 2 ! 2 ! } = 6 ; } \end{array}$ , and as there are $\frac { n ( n - 1 ) } { 2 }$ di¤erent such terms with $j \neq k _ { : }$ , the total count is $3 n ( n - 1 )$ . Combining produces the third expression: 

$$
\mathrm{E} \left[ \frac {1}{n ^ {2}} \left[ \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} Y _ {i} Y _ {k} \right] ^ {2} \right] = \frac {1}{n} \mu_ {4} + \frac {3 (n - 1)}{n} \sigma^ {4}.
$$

Finally, the three expressions are combined to 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \operatorname{E} \left[ \left[ \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} (X _ {j} - \hat {X}) ^ {2} \right] ^ {2} \right] = n \mu_ {4} + n (n - 1) \sigma^ {4} - 2 \mu_ {4} - 2 (n - 1) \sigma^ {4} + \frac {1}{n} \mu_ {4} + \frac {3 (n - 1)}{n} \sigma^ {4} \\ = \bigg (n - 2 + \frac {1}{n} \bigg) \mu_ {4} + \bigg [ (n - 2) (n - 1) + \frac {3 (n - 1)}{n} \bigg ] \sigma^ {4}. \end{array}
$$

Dividing by $( n - 1 ) ^ { 2 }$ produces $\operatorname { E } [ { \hat { V } } ^ { 2 } ]$ , and subtracting $( \operatorname { E } [ { \hat { V } } ] ) ^ { 2 } = \sigma ^ { 4 }$ gives the final result: 

$$
\operatorname{Var} [ \hat {V} ] = \frac {1}{n} \mu_ {4} - \frac {n - 3}{n (n - 1)} \sigma^ {4},\tag{7.86}
$$

as well as the associated result for $\hat { \sigma } _ { M L E } ^ { 2 }$ , interpreted as a random variable, by multiplying (7.86) by $\textstyle { \frac { ( n - 1 ) ^ { 2 } } { n ^ { 2 } } }$ 

$$
\operatorname{Var} \left[ \hat {\sigma} _ {M L E} ^ {2} \right] = \frac {(n - 1) ^ {2}}{n ^ {3}} \mu_ {4} - \frac {(n - 1) (n - 3)}{n ^ {3}} \sigma^ {4}.\tag{7.87}
$$

## Other Sample Moments

Higher Order Moments Due to the messiness of estimating the central moments, as observed for the estimates above related to the sample variance, we focus on estimates of the moments $\mu _ { k } ^ { \prime }$ . Given an independent and identically distributed sample $\{ X _ { j } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { n }$ , the general higher sample moment estimation formula is 

$$
\hat {\mu} _ {k} ^ {\prime} = \frac {1}{n} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} X _ {j} ^ {k}.\tag{7.88}
$$

The derivations of the following are assigned in exercise 13: 

$$
\mathrm{E} [ \hat {\mu} _ {k} ^ {\prime} ] = \mu_ {k} ^ {\prime},\tag{7.89a}
$$

$$
\mathrm{Var} [ \hat {\mu} _ {k} ^ {\prime} ] = \frac {1}{n} [ \mu_ {2 k} ^ {\prime} - (\mu_ {k} ^ {\prime}) ^ {2} ],\tag{7.89b}
$$

provided that $\mu _ { k } ^ { \prime }$ and $\mu _ { 2 k } ^ { \prime }$ exist. 

Remark 7.48 The identities in exercise 12 between theoretical moments $\{ \mu _ { k } ^ { \prime } \}$ and $\{ \mu _ { k } \}$ do not apply in the context ofsample moments because, in that context, $\mu _ { k }$ is $t y p \textmd { - }$ ically defined relative to the sample mean X and not the theoretical mean<sup>^</sup> $\mu .$ These formulas do apply if central moments are defined relative to the theoretical mean $\mu ,$ but this is impractical in most circumstances, as noted above. 

Moment-Generating Function Given an independent and identically distributed sample $\{ X _ { j } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { n }$ , the sample moment-generating function estimation formula is 

$$
\hat {M} _ {X} (t) = \frac {1}{n} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} e ^ {t X _ {j}}.\tag{7.90}
$$

The function $\hat { M } _ { X } ( t )$ can be interpreted as a random variable on ${ \mathcal { S } } ^ { n }$ for each t. 

In exercise 34 are assigned the following: 

$$
\operatorname{E} [ \hat {M} _ {X} (t) ] = M _ {X} (t),\tag{7.91a}
$$

$$
\operatorname{Var} \left[ \hat {M} _ {X} (t) \right] = \frac {1}{n} \left[ M _ {X} (2 t) - M _ {X} ^ {2} (t) \right].\tag{7.91b}
$$

These functions are interpreted as valid for each t, provided that $M _ { X } ( t )$ and $M _ { X } ( 2 t )$ exist. 

## 7.6 Discrete Probability Density Functions

Clearly, a random variable X conveys some but not all of the information about a sample space $s ,$ its complete collection of events $\mathcal { E } ,$ and associated probability measure Pr, and it transfers this information to a collection of real numbers $\{ x _ { j } \}$ in the range of the random variable. In particular, a random variable allows us to think of the values in the range of $X$ as ‘‘occurring’’ with certain probabilities. This is a good way to proceed for mathematical analysis because we can then study probability density functions and their properties objectively without having to reference the context of the original sample space or defining random variable. Indeed it is common to use a generic random variable X to define a given p.d.f., without reference to the defining sample space or events or to the functional form of $X ,$ in order to provide an objective language for investigating the properties of $f ( x )$ 

However, it is important to remember that the number $x _ { j }$ occurs with probability $f ( x _ { j } )$ not in isolation but because the event defined by $X ^ { - 1 } ( x _ { j } ) \in \mathcal { E }$ occurs with probability $\operatorname* { P r } [ X ^ { - 1 } ( x _ { j } ) ]$ in a given sample space S. 

In this section we list several of the most common examples of discrete p.d.f.s. Of course, there are infinitely many possible probability functions. In the finite case, if $\{ x _ { j } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } \subset \mathbb { R }$ and $\{ f _ { j } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { n }$ is any collection of real numbers, then one can define a p.d.f. by 

$$
f (x _ {j}) = \frac {| f _ {j} |}{\sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} | f _ {k} |}.
$$

In the countably infinite case, if $\{ x _ { j } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { \infty } \subset \mathbb { R }$ and $\{ f _ { j } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { \infty } \in l _ { 1 }$ as defined in chapter $^ { 6 , }$ then a p.d.f. can analogously be defined by 

$$
f (x _ {j}) = \frac {| f _ {j} |}{\sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} | f _ {k} |}.
$$

Consequently any l<sub>1</sub>-sequence can be used to define a p.d.f. in a countably infinite context. Of course, we use $| f _ { j } |$ to ensure that $f ( x _ { j } ) \geq 0$ for all $j .$ In either the finite or countable case, the associated c.d.f.s are then defined by (7.22). 

While these general constructions are useful to exemplify the range of potential p.d.f.s and some of their properties, there is a far more limited number of examples found in common practice. 

## 7.6.1 Discrete Rectangular Distribution

The simplest probability density that can be imagined is one that assumes the same value on every sample point. The domain of this distribution is arbitrary but is conventionally taken as ${ \textstyle \left\{ { \frac { j } { n } } \right\} } _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } \operatorname { o r } \left\{ { \frac { j } { n + 1 } } \right\} _ { j = 0 } ^ { n } ,$ , so in either case Dmn $[ f ( x ) ] \subset [ 0 , 1 ]$ , where ‘‘Dmn’’ denotes the domain of the function as in definition 2.23. Rather than present two sets of formulas, we focus on the former definition and leave it as a general exercise to translate these to the latter setting if needed. 

For a given $n ,$ the p.d.f. of the discrete rectangular distribution, sometimes called the discrete uniform distribution, is defined on $\left\{ { \frac { j } { n } } \right\} _ { j = 1 } ^ { n }$ by 

$$
f ^ {R} \left(\frac {j}{n}\right) = \frac {1}{n}, \quad j = 1, 2, \dots , n.\tag{7.92}
$$

It is a relatively easy calculation to derive the mean and variance of this distribution, using the formulas 

$$
\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} j = \frac {n (n + 1)}{2},
$$

$$
\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} j ^ {2} = \frac {n (n + 1) (2 n + 1)}{6},
$$

which can be easily proved by mathematical induction. Implementing the necessary algebra, we derive 

$$
\mu_ {R} = \frac {n + 1}{2 n},\tag{7.93a}
$$

$$
\sigma_ {R} ^ {2} = \frac {n ^ {2} - 1}{1 2 n ^ {2}}.\tag{7.93b}
$$

Similarly the moment-generating function can be calculated as the sum of a geometric series, since $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { 1 } { n } \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } e ^ { j t / n } = \frac { 1 } { n } \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } ( e ^ { t / n } ) ^ { j } } \end{array}$ , producing 

$$
M _ {R} (t) = \frac {e ^ {[ 1 + (1 / n) ] t} - e ^ {t / n}}{n (e ^ {t / n} - 1)}.\tag{7.94}
$$

It is apparent from (7.93) that as $n  \infty , \mu _ { R }  \frac { 1 } { 2 }$ and $\sigma _ { R } ^ { 2 } \to \frac { 1 } { 1 2 }$ . Less apparent is what happens in the limit for the moment-generating function, due to the denominator, as it is clear that the numerator approaches $e ^ { t } - 1$ . For the denominator we once again use the series expression for the exponential, to be proved in chapter 9, that $\begin{array} { r } { e ^ { i / n } = \sum _ { j = 0 } ^ { \infty } \left( \frac { t } { n } \right) ^ { j } \frac { 1 } { j ! } } \end{array}$ . From this the denominator is seen to equal $t + { \frac { h _ { n } ( t ) } { n } }$ , where $h _ { n } ( t )$ is bounded as $n  \infty$ , so this denominator is seen to approach t. Hence as $n  \infty$ ， $\begin{array} { r } { M _ { R } ( t ) \longrightarrow \frac { e ^ { t } - 1 } { t } } \end{array}$ . As will be seen in chapter 10, these limiting values are the corresponding expressions for the continuous counterpart to the rectangular distribution defined on ½0; 1. 

One of the most important applications of this distribution will be to the problem of generating random samples from other distributions, a problem that is addressed in section 7.7 below. 

This distribution can also be defined on an arbitrary closed interval $[ a , b ]$ , generalizing the model above defined on ½0; 1. The probability density is now defined on $\displaystyle \sum _ { \mathrm { o b t a i n } } ( a + ( b - a ) \frac { j } { n } \bigg \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { n }$ with values as in (7.92), and from (7.55) and (7.56) or directly we 

$$
\mu_ {R _ {a, b}} = \frac {n - 1}{2 n} a + \frac {n + 1}{2 n} b,\tag{7.95a}
$$

$$
\sigma_ {R _ {a, b}} ^ {2} = (b - a) ^ {2} \frac {n ^ {2} - 1}{1 2 n ^ {2}}.\tag{7.95b}
$$

Limits as $n  \infty$ are then $\begin{array} { r } { \mu _ { R _ { a , b } } = \frac { a + b } { 2 } } \end{array}$ and $\begin{array} { r } { \sigma _ { R _ { a , b } } ^ { 2 } = \frac { \left( b - a \right) ^ { 2 } } { 1 2 } } \end{array}$ 

## 7.6.2 Binomial Distribution

For a given p, $0 < p < 1$ , the standard binomial random variable is defined as $X _ { 1 } ^ { B } : { \mathcal { S } } \to \{ 0 , 1 \}$ , where the associated p.d.f. is defined on f0; 1g by $f ( 1 ) = p _ { ; }$ 2 $f ( 0 ) = p ^ { \prime } \equiv 1 - p$ . This is often economically expressed as 

$$
X _ {1} ^ {B} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 1, & \operatorname * {P r} = p, \\ 0, & \operatorname * {P r} = p ^ {\prime}, \end{array} \right.
$$

or to emphasize the associated p.d.f., 

$$
f (X _ {1} ^ {B}) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} p, & X _ {1} ^ {B} = 1, \\ p ^ {\prime}, & X _ {1} ^ {B} = 0. \end{array} \right.\tag{7.96}
$$

A simple application for this random variable is the single coin flip so that ${ \mathcal { S } } =$ $\{ H , T \}$ , and where a probability measure has been defined on $\mathcal { S }$ by $\Pr ( H ) = p$ and $\Pr ( T ) = p ^ { \prime }$ so that $X _ { 1 } ^ { B } ( H ) \equiv 1$ and $X _ { 1 } ^ { B } ( T ) \equiv 0$ . This random variable is sometimes referred to as a Bernoulli trial, and the associated c.d.f. as the Bernoulli distribution, after Jakob Bernoulli (1654–1705). 

This standard formulation is then easily transformed to a shifted standard binomial random variable: $Y _ { 1 } ^ { B } = b + ( a - b ) X _ { 1 } ^ { B }$ , which is defined as 

$$
Y _ {1} ^ {B} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} a, & \operatorname * {P r} = p, \\ b, & \operatorname * {P r} = p ^ {\prime}, \end{array} \right.
$$

where the example of $a = 1 , b = - 1$ , is common in discrete stock price modeling. 

Similarly this model can be extended to accommodate sample spaces of n-coin flips, producing the general binomial random variable, which now has two parameters, $p$ and $n \in \mathbb { N }$ . That is, $\mathcal { S } = \{ ( F _ { 1 } F _ { 2 } \ldots F _ { n } )$ j all $F _ { j } = H$ or Tg, and $X _ { n } ^ { B }$ is defined as the ‘‘head-counting’’ random variable: 

$$
X _ {n} ^ {B} (F _ {1} F _ {2} \dots F _ {n}) = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} X _ {1} ^ {B} (F _ {j}).
$$

It is apparent that $X _ { n } ^ { B }$ assumes values $0 , 1 , 2 , \ldots , n ,$ and that using the combinatoria analysis above, the associated probabilities are given by 

$$
X _ {n} ^ {B} = \left\{j; \operatorname * {P r} = \binom {n} {j} p ^ {j} (1 - p) ^ {n - j}, \qquad j = 0, 1, \ldots , n, \right.
$$

or to emphasize the associated p.d.f., 

$$
f ^ {B} (j) = \binom {n} {j} p ^ {j} (1 - p) ^ {n - j}, \qquad j = 0, 1, \ldots , n.\tag{7.97}
$$

To derive these probabilities, we observe that if $\left( F _ { 1 } F _ { 2 } \ldots F _ { n } \right) \in { \mathcal { S } }$ is any sample point with $j \ H \mathbf { s } ,$ , then $\operatorname* { P r } ( F _ { 1 } F _ { 2 } \ldots F _ { n } ) = p ^ { j } { ( 1 - p ) } ^ { n - j }$ . Moreover, for any $j ,$ there are $\binom { n } { j }$ such sample points. Consequently the event $[ X _ { n } ^ { B } ] ^ { - 1 } ( j )$ in $\mathcal { E }$ has probability as given in (7.97). Of course, $\textstyle \sum _ { j = 0 } ^ { n } f ^ { B } ( j ) = 1$ by the binomial theorem in (7.15) with $a = p$ and $b = p ^ { \prime }$ , since then $a + b = 1$
