$$

and hence $g ^ { \prime } ( 0 ) = 0 .$ . Combining, we obtain the result: 

$I f g ( x ) = | x | ^ { p } , p > 1$ , then 

$$
g ^ {\prime} (x) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} p | x | ^ {p - 1}, & x \geq 0, \\ - p | x | ^ {p - 1}, & x \leq 0. \end{array} \right.\tag{9.20}
$$

A Discussion of e 

The simplest approach to deriving the numerical value of e involves two steps: 

Step 1. Define e by 

$$
e = \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{n !}.
$$

That this summation converges follows directly from chapter 6 and the ratio test. Since $\begin{array} { r } { b _ { n } = \frac { 1 } { n ! } } \end{array}$ , we see that as $n \to \infty$ 2 

$$
\frac {b _ {n + 1}}{b _ {n}} = \frac {1}{n + 1} \rightarrow 0.
$$

It is also apparent that $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { 1 } { n ! } \leq \frac { 1 } { 2 ^ { n - 1 } } } \end{array}$ for $n \geq 1$ , so by evaluation of the geometric series, 

$$
e = 1 + \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{n !}
$$

$$
\leq 1 + \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{2 ^ {n}} = 3.
$$

In fact 

$$
e \approx 2. 7 1 8 2 8 1 8 2 8 4 5 9 \dots .\tag{9.21}
$$

Step 2. Define $\textstyle a _ { n } = { \bigl ( } 1 + { \frac { 1 } { n } } { \bigr ) } ^ { n }$ as in (9.19) of case 7 of example 9.80 above. We now show that $a _ { n } \to e . \mathrm { \bf ~ B y }$ the binomial theorem, 

$$
a _ {n} = \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n} {\binom {n} {j}} \frac {1}{n ^ {j}}
$$

$$
= 1 + \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} \left[ \prod_ {k = 0} ^ {j - 1} \left(1 - \frac {k}{n}\right) \right] \frac {1}{j !}.
$$

From this result we conclude that since $\begin{array} { r } { \prod _ { k = 0 } ^ { j - 1 } \bigl ( 1 - \frac { k } { n } \bigr ) \le 1 } \end{array}$ 2 

$$
a _ {n} \leq e _ {n} <   e,
$$

where $\begin{array} { r } { e _ { n } = \sum _ { j = 0 } ^ { n } \frac { 1 } { j ! } } \end{array}$ is the partial sum that converges to e above. It is also apparent that 

$$
a _ {n} <   a _ {n + 1},
$$

since $a _ { n + 1 }$ has one more positive term in the summation above, and for the other terms, the coe‰cients of $\left\{ { \frac { 1 } { j ! } } \right\} _ { j = 1 } ^ { n }$ increase from $\textstyle \prod _ { k = 0 } ^ { j - 1 } \left( 1 - { \frac { k } { n } } \right)$ to $\textstyle \prod _ { k = 0 } ^ { j - 1 } \left( 1 - { \frac { k } { n + 1 } } \right)$ . Because $a _ { n }$ is an increasing sequence and is bounded above by e, this sequence converges by chapter 5 to a say, where $a \leq e .$ . To see that $a = e ,$ , note that for $m > n$ 

$$
a _ {m} = 1 + \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {m} \left[ \prod_ {k = 0} ^ {j - 1} \left(1 - \frac {k}{m}\right) \right] \frac {1}{j !}
$$

$$
> 1 + \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} \left[ \prod_ {k = 0} ^ {j - 1} \left(1 - \frac {k}{m}\right) \right] \frac {1}{j !}.
$$

Letting $m  \infty$ , we conclude that since $a _ { m } \to a$ and $\textstyle \prod _ { k = 0 } ^ { j - 1 } \bigl ( 1 - \frac { k } { m } \bigr ) \to 1$ 2 

$$
a \geq e _ {n}.
$$

Combining, we have 

$$
a _ {n} \leq e _ {n} \leq a,
$$

and hence $a _ { n } \to e$ as desired. 

## 9.3.4 Properties of Derivatives

One important and well-known result for di¤erentiable functions is the following mean value theorem, which often goes under the moniker of the MVT. Graphically, recalling (9.9), the MVT states that if $f ( x )$ satisfies the given properties on $[ a , b ]$ , then there is a point $c \in ( a , b )$ so that the slope of the tangent line to $y = f ( x )$ at $c ,$ or $f ^ { \prime } ( c )$ , equals the slope between the endpoints of the graph of $f ( x )$ on $[ a , b ]$ . The endpoints are, of course, $( a , f ( a ) )$ and $( b , f ( b ) )$ . 

Proposition 9.83 (Mean Value Theorem) $H f ( x )$ is di¤erentiable on $( a , b )$ and continuous on $[ a , b ]$ , then there is a number $c \in ( a , b )$ , so that 

$$
f ^ {\prime} (c) = \frac {f (b) - f (a)}{b - a}.\tag{9.22}
$$

Proof Define a new function 

$$
g (x) = f (x) - \frac {f (b) - f (a)}{b - a} (x - a).
$$

Then $g ( a ) = g ( b ) = f ( a )$ , and $\begin{array} { r } { g ^ { \prime } ( x ) = f ^ { \prime } ( x ) - \frac { f ( b ) - f ( a ) } { b - a } } \end{array}$ , so the proof follows if we can show that there is a $c \in ( a , b )$ with $g ^ { \prime } ( c ) = 0$ . The next proposition provides this conclusion. n 

Proposition 9.84 (Rolle’s Theorem) $H g ( x )$ is di¤erentiable on $( a , b )$ and continuous on $[ a , b ]$ , with $g ( a ) = g ( b )$ , then there is a number $c \in ( a , b )$ , so that $g ^ { \prime } ( c ) = 0 .$ 

Proof If $g ( x )$ is constant on $[ a , b ]$ , then the conclusion follows for all $c \in ( a , b )$ . If not constant, then as a continuous function on $[ a , b ] , g ( x )$ must achieve both its maximum and minimum value on this interval. Since $g ( x )$ is assumed to be nonconstant and $g ( a ) = g ( b )$ , at least one of these must occur within $( a , b )$ , and we denote this value by c. Now, if $g ( c )$ is a maximum, we conclude that 

$$
\frac {g (x) - g (c)}{x - c} \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \leq 0, & x \geq c, \\ \geq 0, & x \leq c, \end{array} \right.
$$

and with the opposite inequalities at a minimum. Since the limit must exist as $x \longrightarrow c ,$ and equal $g ^ { \prime } ( c )$ , we conclude that the only possible value for this limit is 0. n 

## Remark 9.85

1. With the aid ofthe mean value theorem, we return to the point made in section $9 . 2 . 6$ on Ho¨lder continuity, that being, $i f f ( x )$ is Ho¨lder continuous of order $\alpha > 1$ on an interval $( a , b )$ , then $f ( x ) = c ,$ , a constant on this interval. To see this, first note that $i f$ $f ( x )$ has this order of continuity at $x _ { 0 . }$ , then 

$$
\left| \frac {f (x) - f (x _ {0})}{\Delta x} \right| = O (\Delta x ^ {\alpha - 1}),
$$

and hence $f ^ { \prime } ( x _ { 0 } ) = 0 .$ . Consequently, $i f f ( x )$ has this order ofcontinuity throughout an interval $( a , b )$ , then $f ^ { \prime } ( x ) = 0$ for all $x \in ( a , b )$ . By the MVT, for any interval $[ c , d ] \subset$ $( a , b )$ there is $e \in [ c , d ]$ with ${ \frac { \check { f } ( d ) - f ( c ) } { d - c } } = \check { f } ^ { \prime } ( e )$ , and we conclude from $f ^ { \prime } ( e ) = 0$ that ${ f ( d ) = f ( c ) , s o f ( x ) }$ is constant. Ofcourse, there is no such conclusion $i f f ( x )$ satisfies this Ho¨lder condition at an isolated point, as the functions $f ( x ) = x ^ { \alpha } f o r \alpha > 1$ demonstrate at $x = 0$ 

2. Another consequence of (9.22) noted in item 1 is that if $f ^ { \prime } ( x ) \equiv 0$ on an interval $( a , b )$ , then for any $c , d \in ( a , b )$ , we must have that $f ( c ) = f ( d )$ . In other words, the only functions with identically 0 first derivatives are the constant functions. 

The proof of Rolle’s theorem produces a necessary condition on a point $c \in ( a , b )$ to be a relative maximum or a relative minimum of $f ( x )$ on $[ a , b ]$ , but first a definition. 

Definition 9.86 A point c is a relative minimum of a function $f ( x )$ if there is an open interval I, with $c \in I ,$ so that for all $x \in I , f ( c ) \leq f ( x )$ . The point c is a relative maximum of $f ( x )$ if there is an open interval I containing c so that for all $x \in I ,$ $f ( c ) \geq f ( x )$ 

When $f ( x )$ is a di¤erentiable function, it is often easy to find all possible candidates for relative minimums and relative maximums. Specifically, at any such point, $f ^ { \prime } ( c ) = 0 \quad$ 

Proposition 9.87 If c is a relative maximum or relative minimum of $f ( x )$ , and $f ( x )$ is di¤erentiable at c, then $f ^ { \prime } ( c ) = 0$ 

Proof As in the proof of Rolle’s theorem, at a relative minimum, 

$$
\frac {f (x) - f (c)}{x - c} \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \geq 0, & x \geq c, \\ \leq 0, & x \leq c, \end{array} \right.
$$

and the inequalities reverse at a relative maximum. As $x \longrightarrow c ,$ the existence of $f ^ { \prime } ( c )$ implies that these ratios converge to the same value, which must therefore be $0 . \ \equiv$ 

## Example 9.88

1. Note that a di¤erentiable function does not necessarily have $f ^ { \prime } ( x ) = 0$ at a global maximum or global minimum on $[ a , b ] .$ , since such extreme values may occur at an interval endpoint. For example, $f ( x ) = x$ is a simple function that achieves its global maximum and minimum on the endpoints of every closed interval $[ a , b ]$ , and yet $f ^ { \prime } ( x ) \equiv 1$ 

2. Also $f ^ { \prime } ( c ) = 0$ is only a necessary condition for a relative maximum or minimum; it is not su‰cient as the function $f ( x ) = x ^ { 3 }$ exemplifies at $c = 0$ 

Because of the importance of the points at which the derivative of a function is zero, these points warrant a special name. 

Definition 9.89 Given a di¤erentiable function $f ( x )$ , the points for which $f ^ { \prime } ( c ) = 0$ are known as the critical points of $f ( x )$ 

Critical points are the first place one looks to find relative maximums or minimums of a di¤erentiable function. Because such an analysis will only reveal a function’s relative maximums and minimums, for global maximums and minimums on a closed and bounded interval, the second place to be evaluated are the interval’s endpoints. For global maximums and minimums on an open interval, $( a , b )$ , bounded or unbounded, one needs to consider the function’s values as $x \longrightarrow a$ and $x \longrightarrow b ,$ , and in such cases the function may be unbounded, meaning the global maximum (respectively, minimum) is $\infty$ (respectively, <sub>-y</sub>). 

A final simple property, but a useful one to highlight, was noted in the proof of the derivative formula for the inverse function in proposition 9.77. Its proof is assigned as exercise 7, and will be omitted. 

Proposition 9.90 $H f ( x )$ is di¤erentiable at $x _ { 0 } , f ^ { \prime } ( x _ { 0 } ) \neq 0 .$ , and $f ^ { \prime } ( x )$ is continuous in an open interval containing $x _ { 0 }$ then there is an open interval about $x _ { 0 } .$ , say $\begin{array} { r } { I = \left( x _ { 0 } - a _ { : } \right. } \end{array}$ $x _ { 0 } + a )$ for some $a > 0$ , so that on $I , f ( x )$ is one-to-one and monotonic. Specifically, if $x , y \in I$ and $x < y ,$ then 

$$
f ^ {\prime} (x _ {0}) > 0 \Rightarrow f (x) <   f (y),
$$

$$
f ^ {\prime} (x _ {0}) <   0 \Rightarrow f (x) > f (y).
$$

## 9.3.5 Improving an Approximation II

Another significant conclusion that can be drawn from the mean value theorem is a numerical refinement of the rate of convergence of $f ( x )$ to $f ( x _ { 0 } )$ in the case where $f ( x )$ has a bounded derivative. Specifically, if $M = \operatorname* { m a x } \{ f ^ { \prime } ( x ) | x \in ( a , b ) \}$ , then for any $x , x _ { 0 } \in ( a , b )$ , we have from (9.10) and the triangle inequality that 

$$
| f (x) - f \left(x _ {0}\right) | \leq M | x - x _ {0} |.\tag{9.23}
$$

While this bound is in theory less powerful than (9.7), which we rewrite here for comparability, 

$$
| f (x) - f (x _ {0}) | \leq f ^ {\prime} (x _ {0}) | x - x _ {0} | + o (| x - x _ {0} |),
$$

in practice, it can be more valuable when M is easily estimated, since this inequality works uniformly for any x and $x _ { 0 }$ in the interval, rather than only at a point, $x _ { 0 }$ . This estimate also avoids the extra Little o term that, while useful when we have $\Delta x \to 0 .$ 2 is not useful for numerical estimates when $\Delta x$ is fixed and finite, since its exact formula is unknown. 

Also note that by rewriting (9.7) with $a = f ^ { \prime } ( x _ { 0 } )$ , we achieve the following approximation: 

$$
f (x) = f \left(x _ {0}\right) + f ^ {\prime} \left(x _ {0}\right) \Delta x + o (\Delta x),\tag{9.24}
$$

where as usual, $x = x _ { 0 } + \Delta x$ . We will see below that this is a special case of a Taylor series expansion of $f ( x )$ 

Comparing (9.24) with (9.9), we identify the error between the tangent line approximation and the graph of the function to be $o ( \Delta x )$ 

## 9.3.6 Higher Order Derivatives

In order to pursue higher order approximations to $f ( x )$ near $x _ { 0 }$ , we define the following notion: 

Definition 9.91 For each integer $n > 1$ , the nth derivative of $f ( x )$ at $x _ { 0 } .$ , denoted $\begin{array} { r } { f ^ { ( n ) } ( x _ { 0 } ) , o r , \frac { d ^ { n } f } { d x ^ { n } } \bigg | _ { x = x _ { 0 } } , } \end{array}$ is defined iteratively by 

$$
f ^ {(n)} (x _ {0}) \equiv \lim _ {\Delta x \to 0} \frac {f ^ {(n - 1)} (x) - f ^ {(n - 1)} (x _ {0})}{\Delta x},\tag{9.25}
$$

when this limit exists. One then says that $f ( x )$ is n-times di¤erentiable at $x _ { 0 }$ , or on an interval $( a , b )$ , and so forth. $H f ^ { ( n ) } ( x _ { 0 } )$ exists for all n, we say that $f ( x )$ is infinitely di¤erentiable at $x _ { 0 } .$ , or infinitely di¤erentiable on an interval, and so forth. The existence of the nth derivative of $f ( x )$ can also be expressed in a way that is analogous to $( 9 . I O )$ 

$$
f ^ {(n - 1)} (x _ {0} + \Delta x) - f ^ {(n - 1)} (x _ {0}) = \Delta x (f ^ {(n)} (x _ {0}) + \varepsilon_ {f ^ {(n - 1)}} (x _ {0} + \Delta x)).
$$

Note that if $f ( x )$ is n-times di¤erentiable at $x _ { 0 }$ , then by proposition 9.72 each of the first $( n - 1 )$ derivatives must be continuous at $x _ { 0 }$ . Also note above that a function’s nth derivative is calculated sequentially, by calculating in turn the function’s derivatives, first, then second, and so on. Below we investigate numerical estimation of derivatives that are developed directly from values of the function. 

Example 9.92 Let $f ( x ) = x ^ { N } .$ , where N is a positive integer. Then as was shown in example 9.71 above, $f ^ { \prime } ( x ) = N x ^ { N - 1 }$ $B y$ iteration, we derive that 

$$
\frac {d x ^ {N}}{d x ^ {n}} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \frac {N !}{(N - n) !} x ^ {N - n}, & n \leq N, \\ 0, & n > N, \end{array} \right.
$$

where we recall below the factorial notation and related binomial coe‰cients. 

## Definition 9.93

1. If N is a positive integer, then N!, or Nfactorial is defined as 

$$
N! = N (N - 1) (N - 2) \dots 2 \cdot 1,
$$

and also $0 ! = 1$ (see chapter 10, the gamma distribution, for a compelling motivation for the definition $o f 0 ! )$ . 

2. If N and M are nonnegative integers, $0 \leq M \leq N _ { \cdot }$ , the binomial coe‰cient, $\textstyle { \binom { N } { M } }$ is defined as 

$$
\binom {N} {M} = \frac {N !}{M ! (N - M) !}.
$$

## 9.3.7 Improving an Approximation III: Taylor Series Approximations

Generalizing the analysis above that led to (9.24), we introduce next the general Taylor series. To this end, assume that we want to approximate $f ( x )$ with an nth order polynomial, generalizing the first order approximation in (9.24). In other words, the goal is to approximate $f ( x )$ by 

$$
f (x) \approx \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n} a _ {j} (x - x _ {0}) ^ {j},
$$

where here we express $\Delta x$ as $x - x _ { 0 }$ for specificity below. 

If we assume that $f ( x )$ is n-times di¤erentiable, we can di¤erentiate this expression using example 9.92 above, and substitute $x = x _ { 0 }$ to solve for the coe‰cients $a _ { j }$ . For example, 

$$
f (x _ {0}) = \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n} a _ {j} (x _ {0} - x _ {0}) ^ {j} = a _ {0},
$$

$$
f ^ {\prime} (x _ {0}) = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} j a _ {j} (x _ {0} - x _ {0}) ^ {j - 1} = a _ {1},
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} f ^ {(2)} (x _ {0}) = \sum_ {j = 2} ^ {n} j (j - 1) a _ {j} (x _ {0} - x _ {0}) ^ {j - 2} = 2 a _ {2}, \\ \vdots \end{array}
$$

$$
f ^ {(m)} (x _ {0}) = \sum_ {j = m} ^ {n} \frac {j !}{(j - m) !} a _ {j} (x _ {0} - x _ {0}) ^ {j - m} = m! a _ {m} \quad \text {   for   } m \leq n.
$$

From this calculation we derive the nth-order Taylor polynomial for $f ( x )$ centered at $x _ { 0 }$ : 

$$
f (x) \approx \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n} \frac {1}{j !} f ^ {(j)} (x _ {0}) (x - x _ {0}) ^ {j}.\tag{9.26}
$$

This expansion is named for Brook Taylor (1685–1731) who published the approximation result in (9.26) in the early 1700s, although it was apparently discovered some time earlier by James Gregory (1638–1675). When $x _ { 0 } = 0$ , this series approximation is sometimes referred to as a Maclaurin series, named for Colin Maclaurin (1698– $1 7 4 6 )$ , who applied this idea to trigonometric functions. 

As a first application we derive the nth-order Taylor polynomial for $e ^ { x }$ , first referenced in chapter $6$ and applied in chapter 7. 

Example 9.94 With $f ( x ) = e ^ { x }$ , and $x _ { 0 } = 0 _ { \cdot }$ , we have that $f ^ { ( n ) } ( x _ { 0 } ) = e ^ { x _ { 0 } } = 1$ for all $n ,$ and so 

$$
e ^ {x} \approx \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n} \frac {1}{j !} x ^ {j}.
$$

We next investigate the error in the approximation in (9.26). Of course, if $f ( x )$ is a polynomial of degree $n ,$ the nth-order Taylor polynomial will exactly reproduce $f ( x )$ In fact from (9.26) it is apparent that for any such polynomial, the coe‰cient of $x ^ { j }$ equals the jth-derivative of the polynomial divided by $j ! ,$ where these derivatives are evaluated at $x = 0$ . In general, however, there will be a remainder, also called the error term. 

We now investigate one property of this remainder. 

Proposition 9.95 $H f ( x )$ is n-times di¤erentiable on an interval $( a , b )$ , with $f ^ { ( j ) } ( x )$ continuous on $\left[ a , b \right] f o r j \leq n - 1$ , then for $x , x _ { 0 } \in [ a , b ]$ 

$$
f (x) = \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n} \frac {1}{j !} f ^ {(j)} (x _ {0}) (x - x _ {0}) ^ {j} + O (\Delta x ^ {n}),\tag{9.27}
$$

where $\Delta x = x - x _ { 0 }$ . In addition, if $f ^ { ( n ) } ( x )$ is continuous on $[ a , b ] .$ , then the error improves slightly to 

$$
f (x) = \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n} \frac {1}{j !} f ^ {(j)} (x _ {0}) (x - x _ {0}) ^ {j} + o (\Delta x ^ {n}).\tag{9.28}
$$

Proof For $x , x _ { 0 } \in [ a , b ]$ given, with $x _ { 0 } < x$ for specificity, define the constant $A \equiv$ $A ( x , x _ { 0 } )$ , so that 

$$
f (x) = \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} \frac {1}{j !} f ^ {(j)} (x _ {0}) (x - x _ {0}) ^ {j} + A \frac {(x - x _ {0}) ^ {n}}{n !},
$$

and define the residual function 

$$
g (y) = f (x) - \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} \frac {1}{j !} f ^ {(j)} (y) (x - y) ^ {j} - A \frac {(x - y) ^ {n}}{n !}.
$$

Now by the assumptions of the proposition, $g ( y )$ is continuous on $[ a , b ]$ and di¤erentiable on $( a , b )$ . Also $g ( x ) = g ( x _ { 0 } ) = 0$ . So by Rolle’s theorem, there is a value $c \in$ $( x _ { 0 } , x )$ so that $g ^ { \prime } ( c ) = 0$ . A calculation, using the product rule for derivatives, produces $g ^ { \prime } ( y )$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} g ^ {\prime} (y) = - \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} \frac {1}{j !} f ^ {(j + 1)} (y) (x - y) ^ {j} + \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n - 1} \frac {1}{(j - 1) !} f ^ {(j)} (y) (x - y) ^ {j - 1} \\ \qquad + A \frac {(x - y) ^ {n - 1}}{(n - 1) !}. \end{array}
$$

A careful look at the two summations reveals that the first $n - 1$ terms of the first sum cancel with the $n - 1$ terms of the second, leaving 

$$
g ^ {\prime} (y) = - \frac {1}{(n - 1) !} f ^ {(n)} (y) (x - y) ^ {n - 1} + A \frac {(x - y) ^ {n - 1}}{(n - 1) !}.
$$

The conclusion of Rolle’s theorem, that there is a $c \in ( x _ { 0 } , x )$ so that $g ^ { \prime } ( c ) = 0$ , can be rewritten as 

$$
f ^ {(n)} (c) = A.
$$

Hence we have that for some $c \in ( x _ { 0 } , x )$ ， 

$$
f (x) = \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} \frac {1}{j !} f ^ {(j)} \left(x _ {0}\right) \left(x - x _ {0}\right) ^ {j} + f ^ {(n)} (c) \frac {\left(x - x _ {0}\right) ^ {n}}{n !}.\tag{9.29}
$$

The same conclusion follows if $x _ { 0 } > x .$ . From (9.29) we have then that for some $c \in ( x _ { 0 } , x ) { \mathrm { ~ o r ~ } } c \in ( x , x _ { 0 } )$ 2 

$$
f (x) = \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n} \frac {1}{j !} f ^ {(j)} \left(x _ {0}\right) \left(x - x _ {0}\right) ^ {j} + \left[ f ^ {(n)} (c) - f ^ {(n)} \left(x _ {0}\right) \right] \frac {\left(x - x _ {0}\right) ^ {n}}{n !}.
$$

The error term is seen to be $O ( \Delta x ^ { n } )$ if we only know that $f ^ { ( n ) } ( x )$ exists. However, if $f ^ { ( n ) } ( x )$ is also continuous so that $f ^ { ( n ) } ( c ) - f ^ { ( n ) } ( x _ { 0 } ) \to 0 { \mathrm { ~ a s ~ } } \Delta x \to 0$ , then this error is seen to be $o ( \Delta x ^ { n } )$ 

Notation 9.96 Given $x , x _ { 0 } \in ( a , b )$ , there is a convenient notational devise for identifying a point c that is ‘‘between’’ x and $x _ { 0 . }$ , which is to say that $c \in ( x _ { 0 } , x ) \ i f x _ { 0 } < x ,$ , and $c \in \left( x , x _ { 0 } \right)$ if $x < x _ { 0 }$ . Stated more succinctly, there exists $\theta ,$ with $0 < \theta < 1$ , so that $c = x _ { 0 } + \theta \Delta x .$ where $\Delta x = x - x _ { 0 }$ , and this is used below. 

Example 9.97 From example 9.94, we have that since $e ^ { x }$ is infinitely di¤erentiable, and hence has continuous derivatives of all orders, then for any $n ,$ 

$$
e ^ {x} - \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n} \frac {1}{j !} x ^ {j} = o (x ^ {n}) \quad \text {   as   } x \to 0.
$$

## Analytic Functions

It turns out that in many applications, the Taylor polynomials not only provide highorder approximations to the given function at $x _ { 0 }$ as $\Delta x \to 0$ , but also these polynomials approximate the function everywhere as $n  \infty$ . Such functions are called analytic functions. 

Definition 9.98 A function $f ( x )$ is called analytic in a neighborhood of x<sub>0</sub> if it can be expanded in a convergent Taylor series: 

$$
f (x) = \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{j !} f ^ {(j)} (x _ {0}) (x - x _ {0}) ^ {j},\tag{9.30}
$$

for x in an open interval centered on $x _ { 0 } .$ . In other words, for every x in this interval, 

$$
f (x) = \lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n} \frac {1}{j !} f ^ {(j)} \left(x _ {0}\right)\left(x - x _ {0}\right) ^ {j}.
$$

It is apparent that every polynomial is analytic, since all but a finite number of derivatives satisfy $f ^ { ( j ) } ( x _ { 0 } ) = 0 \qquad $ , as are many familiar functions such as $e ^ { x } { \mathrm { . } }$ ln $x ,$ sin $x ,$ and cos x. Each is analytic everywhere in their respective domains of definition. Proving analyticity, however, requires some new tools, as developed in (9.34) below. The formula (9.27) does not help, even if we know that $f ( x )$ is infinitely differentiable and this formula holds for all n. The reason is that this expression only provides information about the behavior of the Taylor polynomial as $\Delta x \to 0$ . To be analytic at $x _ { 0 }$ requires that $f _ { n } ( x ) \to f ( x )$ as $n  \infty$ for x in a neighborhood of $x _ { 0 }$ , where $f _ { n } ( x )$ denotes the nth-degree Taylor polynomial in (9.26). 

While analyticity requires the existence of infinitely many derivatives, the following classical example demonstrates that it requires more than just this. In other words, infinite di¤erentiability is a necessary condition for a function to be analytic, but it is not a su‰cient condition. 

Example 9.99 Define $f ( x )$ by 

$$
f (x) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} e ^ {- 1 / x ^ {2}}, & x \neq 0, \\ 0, & x = 0. \end{array} \right.
$$

Then every derivative $o f f ( x )$ is a finite sum of terms of the form 

$$
c \frac {e ^ {- 1 / x ^ {2}}}{x ^ {j}}.
$$

So $f ^ { ( n ) } ( x )$ exists for all $x \neq 0$ , but also it is possible to justify that for all n, $f ^ { ( n ) } ( x )  0$ as $x \to 0$ . To see this, substitute $\textstyle y = { \frac { 1 } { x } }$ , obtaining sums of terms of the form $c y ^ { j } e ^ { - y ^ { 2 } }$ and let $y  \infty$ . Then, as $y  \infty$ , since $y ^ { j } < e ^ { y }$ for any $j ,$ we conclude that 

$$
c y ^ {j} e ^ {- y ^ {2}} <   c e ^ {- y (y - 1)} \rightarrow 0 \quad a s y \rightarrow \infty .
$$

In other words, $f ^ { ( n ) } ( 0 ) = 0$ for all $n ,$ and hence the Taylor polynomials evaluated at $x _ { 0 } = 0$ satisfy $f _ { n } ( x ) \equiv 0$ for all n. Consequently we cannot have that $f _ { n } ( x ) \to f ( x )$ as $n  \infty f o r \ x$ in a neighborhood of0, and we conclude that $f ( x )$ is infinitely di¤erentiable but not analytic at 0. 

Note that the definition of analytic above does not require that the Taylor series converge absolutely, only that it converges. This is in contrast to the definition of a power series in chapter 6 for which the interval of convergence and radius of convergence are defined in a way to ensure that these series converge absolutely. However, many analytic functions do indeed converge absolutely, and using chapter 6 methods, we can readily identify two conditions that assure absolute convergence. Both conditions relate to the growth of $\{ f ^ { ( n ) } ( x _ { 0 } ) \}$ as $n  \infty$ 

Proposition 9.100 Let $f ( x )$ be an analytic function given by (9.30) in the interval $| x - x _ { 0 } | < R .$ 

## 1. If

$$
\operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n} \left| \frac {f ^ {(n + 1)} (x _ {0})}{(n + 1) f ^ {(n)} (x _ {0})} \right| = L <   \infty ,\tag{9.31}
$$

then the Taylor series is absolutely convergent for $| x - x _ { 0 } | < R ^ { \prime }$ , where $\begin{array} { r } { R ^ { \prime } = \frac { 1 } { L } } \end{array}$ 

2. If there is an $x ^ { \prime }$ so that 

$$
\left| \frac {f ^ {(n)} (x _ {0})}{n !} (x ^ {\prime} - x _ {0}) ^ {n} \right| \leq C \quad \text {   for   all   } n,\tag{9.32}
$$

then the Taylor series is absolutely convergent for $| x - x _ { 0 } | < R ^ { \prime \prime } .$ , where $R ^ { \prime \prime } =$ $\| x ^ { \prime } - x _ { 0 } \| .$ 

Proof Statement 1 follows from the ratio test in chapter $^ { 6 , }$ which assures absolute convergence if the limit superior of the ratios of successive terms is less than 1. Letting $\begin{array} { r } { c _ { n } \equiv \frac { f ^ { ( n ) } ( x _ { 0 } ) } { n ! } { ( x - x _ { 0 } ) } ^ { n } } \end{array}$ , we write 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \underset {n} {\limsup} \left| \frac {c _ {n + 1}}{c _ {n}} \right| = \underset {n} {\limsup} \left| \frac {f ^ {(n + 1)} (x _ {0})}{(n + 1) f ^ {(n)} (x _ {0})} \right| | x - x _ {0} |, \\ = L | x - x _ {0} |, \end{array}
$$

so absolute convergence is assured if $L | x - x _ { 0 } | < 1$ . Statement 2 follows from the comparison test. Specifically, (9.32) implies that 

$$
\left| \frac {f ^ {(n)} (x _ {0})}{n !} (x - x _ {0}) ^ {n} \right| \leq C \left| \frac {x - x _ {0}}{x ^ {\prime} - x _ {0}} \right| ^ {n}
$$

$$
<   C r ^ {n},
$$

where $r < 1 \ \mathrm { i f } \ | x - x _ { 0 } | < | x ^ { \prime } - x _ { 0 } |$ , and this Taylor series is therefore bounded by a convergent geometric series. n 

A useful corollary of this result is as follows: 

Proposition 9.101 If 

$$
f (x) = \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{j !} f ^ {(j)} (x _ {0}) (x - x _ {0}) ^ {j}, \quad g (x) = \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{j !} g ^ {(j)} (x _ {0}) (x - x _ {0}) ^ {j},
$$

are analytic functions that are absolutely convergent for $| x - x _ { 0 } | < R ,$ then for any $a , b \in \mathbb { R } , h ( x ) \equiv a f ( x ) + b g ( x )$ is analytic, absolutely convergent for $| x - x _ { 0 } | < R ,$ , and $\begin{array} { r } { h ( x ) = \sum _ { j = 0 } ^ { \infty } \frac { 1 } { j ! } h ^ { ( j ) } ( x _ { 0 } ) ( x - x _ { 0 } ) ^ { j } . } \end{array}$ 

Proof That $h ( x )$ is absolutely convergent follows from the triangle inequality and the absolute convergence of $f ( x )$ and $g ( x )$ : 

$$
\left| a \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{j !} f ^ {(j)} (x _ {0}) (x - x _ {0}) ^ {j} + b \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{j !} g ^ {(j)} (x _ {0}) (x - x _ {0}) ^ {j} \right|
$$

$$
\leq | a | \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{j !} | f ^ {(j)} (x _ {0}) (x - x _ {0}) ^ {j} | + | b | \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{j !} | g ^ {(j)} (x _ {0}) (x - x _ {0}) ^ {j} |.
$$

That the Taylor series for $h ( x )$ is given in terms of the derivatives of $h ( x )$ also follows by the absolute convergence of the series 

$$
a \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{j !} f ^ {(j)} (x _ {0}) (x - x _ {0}) ^ {j} + b \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{j !} g ^ {(j)} (x _ {0}) (x - x _ {0}) ^ {j},
$$

which justifies the rearrangement of these terms to 

$$
\sum_ {j = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{j !} [ a f ^ {(j)} (x _ {0}) + b g ^ {(j)} (x _ {0}) ] (x - x _ {0}) ^ {j}.
$$

Remark 9.102 While the Taylor series of an analytic function need not be absolutely convergent, the partial sums of these series are pointwise convergent. Hence these partial sums will be uniformly convergent on any compact set inside the interval of convergence. 

## 9.3.8 Taylor Series Remainder

In this section we present a useful and explicit expression for the remainder term implicit in (9.26) and seen in the development of (9.27) and (9.28). Another expression for this remainder will be seen in section 10.8. 

Defining $f _ { n } ( x )$ as the nth-order Taylor polynomial in (9.26), we write 

$$
f _ {n} (x) = \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n} \frac {1}{j !} f ^ {(j)} (x _ {0}) (x - x _ {0}) ^ {j}.
$$

Proposition 9.95 provides qualitative information on the error term: 

$$
f (x) = f _ {n} (x) + R _ {n} (x).
$$

Summarizing, we have from (9.27) and (9.28) that: 

1. $R _ { n } ( x ) = O ( \Delta x ^ { n } )$ in all cases, requiring only that $f ^ { ( n ) } ( x )$ exists on $( a , b )$ 

2. $R _ { n } ( x ) = o ( \Delta x ^ { n } )$ if $f ^ { ( n ) } ( x )$ is also continuous on this interval. 

Now, what if $f ^ { ( n ) } ( x )$ is also di¤erentiable on this interval? Then proposition 9.95 states that $f ( x )$ can be approximated by $f _ { n + 1 } ( x )$ with an error of $R _ { n + 1 } ( x ) =$ $O ( \Delta x ^ { n + 1 } )$ . Alternatively, the last term in $f _ { n + 1 } ( x )$ can be moved to the error term so that $f ( x )$ can be approximated by $f _ { n } ( x )$ , with an error of 

$$
R _ {n} ^ {\prime} (x) = R _ {n + 1} (x) + \frac {1}{(n + 1) !} f ^ {(n + 1)} (x _ {0}) (x - x _ {0}) ^ {n + 1} = O (\Delta x ^ {n + 1}).
$$

However, it turns out that in this case where we assume that $f ( x )$ has one additional derivative $f ^ { ( n + 1 ) } ( x )$ , an explicit expression for this remainder can also be derived. If this additional derivative is continuous, this explicit expression provides a useful upper bound for this error everywhere in the given interval. This remainder is often used for proving convergence of a Taylor series, as well as providing numerical estimates for given $x _ { 0 }$ and $\Delta x ,$ while the upper bound is used for proving analyticity on a given interval. 

Proposition 9.103 $H f ( x )$ is $( n + 1 )$ -times di¤erentiable on an interval $( a , b )$ , with $f ^ { ( j ) } ( x )$ continuous on $[ a , b ]$ for $j \leq n _ { \ast }$ , and $x , x _ { 0 } \in ( a , b )$ , then there exists $\theta ,$ with $0 < \theta < 1$ , so that 

$$
f (x) = \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n} \frac {1}{j !} f ^ {(j)} \left(x _ {0}\right) \left(x - x _ {0}\right) ^ {j} + \frac {1}{(n + 1) !} f ^ {(n + 1)} (c) \left(x - x _ {0}\right) ^ {n + 1},\tag{9.33}
$$

where $c = x _ { 0 } + \theta \Delta x .$ . In other words, $c$ is between x and $x _ { 0 } ,$ and so $c \in ( x _ { 0 } , x )$ $i f x _ { 0 } < x ,$ and $c \in \left( x , x _ { 0 } \right)$ if $x < x _ { 0 }$ . In addition, if $f ^ { ( n + 1 ) } ( x )$ is continuous on $[ a , b ] .$ , then there exists $M > 0$ so that for all $x , x _ { 0 } \in ( a , b )$ • 

$$
\left| f (x) - \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n} \frac {1}{j !} f ^ {(j)} (x _ {0}) (x - x _ {0}) ^ {j} \right| \leq \frac {M}{(n + 1) !} | x - x _ {0} | ^ {n + 1}.\tag{9.34}
$$

Proof The expression in (9.33) follows immediately from (9.29) in the proof of proposition 9.95. In addition, if $f ^ { ( n + 1 ) } ( x )$ is continuous on $[ a , b ]$ , then from proposition 9.39 this function attains its upper and lower bounds in this interval. Here M denotes the larger of the absolute values of these bounds. n 

Remark 9.104 The remainder term in the Taylor series expansion in (9.33) is known as the Lagrange form of the remainder, after Joseph-Louis Lagrange (1736–1813), who proved the mean value theorem and derived this remainder term from this result. Another form of this remainder, named for Augustin Louis Cauchy, will be developed in section 10.8.

This condition assures that $\scriptstyle \sum _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } ( \theta _ { n } x _ { n } ) ^ { 2 }$ converges, since for $\left. x _ { n } \right. < 1$ ，

\sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \left(\theta_ {n} x _ {n}\right) ^ {2} <   \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} x _ {n} ^ {2} <   \sum | x _ {n} |.

Note that $\begin{array} { r } { x _ { n } = \frac { ( - 1 ) ^ { n } } { \sqrt { n } } } \end{array}$ demonstrates the necessity of this condition of absolute convergence, since although $\textstyle \sum _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } x _ { n } = s < \infty$ , all that can be said about this second summation is that $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } \left( \theta _ { n } x _ { n } \right) ^ { 2 } < \sum _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } \frac { 1 } { n } } \end{array}$ , which is divergent. 

The upper bound for the remainder term is often useful in proving analyticity of a given function. However, we will see that this estimate sometimes fails to provide a proof of convergence of a Taylor series because it is somewhat crude, reflecting the maximum of $f ^ { ( n + 1 ) } ( x )$ on $[ a , b ]$ in general, or more specifically for given $x , x _ { 0 } .$ , the maximum of $f ^ { ( n + 1 ) } ( x )$ on $[ x , x _ { 0 } ]$ or $[ x _ { 0 } , x ]$ . According to (9.29) in the proof of proposition 9.95, we really only need an estimate of the absolute value of $f ^ { ( n + 1 ) } ( x )$ at an intermediate point $c ,$ which is generally unknown. This crudeness can be a problem when this interval maximum is large. 

As noted above, there are other forms of the remainder, and the Cauchy form, which reflects an average of $f ^ { ( n + 1 ) } ( t )$ between x and $x _ { 0 } .$ , will be developed in section 10.8, and seen to succeed in proving analyticity in cases where the Lagrange remainder fails.

## 9.4 Convergence of a Sequence of Derivatives

Expanding the discussion in section 9.2.7 on convergence of a sequence of continuous functions, there is an analogous discussion related to derivatives which we introduce with the following questions: 

Question 1: $\operatorname { I f } f _ { n } ( x )$ is a sequence of di¤erentiable functions, and there is a function $f ( x )$ so that $f _ { n } ( x ) \to f ( x )$ pointwise as $n  \infty$ , must $f ( x )$ be di¤erentiable? 

Question 2: $\operatorname { I f } f ( x )$ in question 1 is di¤erentiable, must $f _ { n } ^ { \prime } ( x )  f ^ { \prime } ( x )$ for every x as $n  \infty ?$ 

Question 3: If $f _ { n } ( x ) \to f ( x )$ uniformly rather than pointwise, do the answers to questions 1 and 2 change? 

Answer: The answer to all three questions is, in general, ‘‘no,’’ and this is easy to exemplify. 

## Example 9.107

$$

$$

Then each $f _ { n } ( x )$ is di¤erentiable, with 

$$

$$

Now $f _ { n } ( x )  f ( x ) \equiv | x |$ , which is not di¤erentiable at $x = 0$ , and for $x \neq 0 , f ^ { \prime } ( x ) = 1$ for $x > 0$ and $f ^ { \prime } ( x ) = - 1 f o r \ x < 0 .$ Also, it is the case that $f _ { n } ^ { \prime } ( x )  f ^ { \prime } ( x ) f o r \ x \neq 0 .$ since $\left| x \right| ^ { 1 / n } \to 1$ as $n  \infty$ for all $x \neq 0$ . This observation provides hope, albeit temporary, that the answer to the second question might be ‘‘yes.’’

Then each $f _ { n } ( x )$ is di¤erentiable, with 

$f _ { n } ^ { \prime } ( x ) = { \sqrt { n } }$ cos nx: 

Now $f _ { n } ( x )  f ( x ) \equiv 0$ for all x since $| \sin n x | \le 1$ , and $f ( x )$ is di¤erentiable everywhere with $f ^ { \prime } ( x ) \equiv 0$ . However, $f _ { n } ^ { \prime } ( 0 ) = { \sqrt { n } }  \infty$ , while $f _ { n } ^ { \prime } ( \pi )$ alternates between $\pm { \sqrt { n } } ,$ and $f _ { n } ^ { \prime } \left( { \frac { \pi } { 2 } } \right)$ cycles through the sequence $\{ 0 , - { \sqrt { n } } , 0 , { \sqrt { n } } \}$ , and so forth. 

3. Finally, although uniform convergence provided a positive result in section 9.2.7 above in terms of preserving continuity it does not help here. Case 1 converges uniformly on compact sets and case 2 converges uniformly, so the same negative conclusions follow. Note, however, that in case 1 the sequence of derivatives, $f _ { n } ^ { \prime } ( x )$ , does not converge uniformly by the Cauchy criterion on any interval that contains 0, since as $n \longrightarrow \infty .$ 

$$
f _ {n} ^ {\prime} (x) \to \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 1, & x > 0, \\ - 1, & x <   0. \end{array} \right.
$$

For case $^ { 2 , }$ the sequence of derivatives $f _ { n } ^ { \prime } ( x )$ does not converge uniformly on any interval. 

Although not the most general statement, the following positive result is adequate in most applications. 

Proposition 9.108 $H f _ { n } ( x )$ is a sequence of continuously di¤erentiable functions and there is a function $f ( x )$ so that on some interval I, $f _ { n } ( x ) \to f ( x )$ uniformly and $f _ { n } ^ { \prime } ( x )$ 

converge uniformly by the Cauchy criterion, then $f ( x )$ is di¤erentiable and $f _ { n } ^ { \prime } ( x ) $ $f ^ { \prime } ( x )$ 

Proof From propositions 9.51 and 9.54 on uniform convergence in section 9.2.7, the assumption that $f _ { n } ^ { \prime } ( x )$ are continuous and converge uniformly by the Cauchy criterion implies that there is a continuous function, $g ( x )$ say, so that $f _ { n } ^ { \prime } ( x )  g ( x )$ uniformly. What is left to prove is that $f ( x )$ is di¤erentiable and $f ^ { \prime } ( x ) = g ( x )$ . To this end, fix $x _ { 0 } \in I .$ and define the ‘‘finite di¤erence functions’’ for $x \neq x _ { 0 } \colon$ 

$$
D _ {n} (x) = \frac {f _ {n} (x) - f _ {n} (x _ {0})}{x - x _ {0}}, \quad D (x) = \frac {f (x) - f (x _ {0})}{x - x _ {0}}.
$$

The assumption that $f _ { n } ( x ) \to f ( x )$ uniformly implies that for $x \neq x _ { 0 }$ 

$$
D _ {n} (x) \to D (x) \quad \text {   as   } n \to \infty .
$$

Since $f _ { n } ( x )$ is di¤erentiable, 

$$
\lim _ {x \to x _ {0}} D _ {n} (x) = f _ {n} ^ {\prime} (x _ {0}) \quad \text {   for   all   } n.
$$

We now show that for fixed $x \neq x _ { 0 } , D _ { n } ( x )$ converges uniformly as $n  \infty$ . This follows in two steps. First o¤, the mean value theorem applied to $f _ { n } ( x ) - f _ { m } ( x )$ yields that for some y between x and $x _ { 0 }$ 

$$
\left| f _ {n} (x) - f _ {m} (x) - f _ {n} \left(x _ {0}\right) + f _ {m} \left(x _ {0}\right) \right| = \left| f _ {n} ^ {\prime} (y) - f _ {m} ^ {\prime} (y) \right| | x - x _ {0} |.
$$

Second, the uniform convergence of $f _ { n } ^ { \prime } ( x )$ means that for any $\epsilon > 0$ there is an $N$ so that for $n , m > N$ and any $y \in I _ { : }$ 

$$
| f _ {n} ^ {\prime} (y) - f _ {m} ^ {\prime} (y) | <   \epsilon .
$$

Combining these steps, we derive that for $n , m > N$ and $x \neq x _ { 0 }$ 2 

$$
\left| D _ {n} (x) - D _ {m} (x) \right| <   \epsilon ,
$$

and so $D _ { n } ( x )$ converges uniformly as $n \to \infty$ for $x \neq x _ { 0 }$ . Combining these pieces, and noting that since $x _ { 0 }$ is a limit point of the set $I - x _ { 0 }$ , the limits below can be reversed because of proposition 9.60. This produces 

$$
\begin{array}{c} f ^ {\prime} (x _ {0}) \equiv \lim _ {x \to x _ {0}} D (x) \\ = \lim _ {x \to x _ {0}} \lim _ {n \to \infty} D _ {n} (x) \end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \lim _ {x \to x _ {0}} D _ {n} (x) \\ = \lim _ {n \to \infty} f _ {n} ^ {\prime} (x _ {0}). \end{array}
$$

## 9.4.1 Series of Functions

The preceding proposition 9.108 generalizes easily to a series of functions. 

Proposition 9.109 $H g _ { j } ( x )$ is a sequence of continuously di¤erentiable functions, and there is a function $g ( x )$ so that on some interval I, $\scriptstyle \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } g _ { j } ( x )$ converges uniformly to $g ( x )$ as $n  \infty$ and $\scriptstyle \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } g _ { j } ^ { \prime } ( x )$ converges uniformly by the Cauchy criterion, then $g ( x )$ is di¤erentiable and ${ \textstyle \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } } { \bar { g } _ { j } ^ { \prime } } ( x ) \to g ^ { \prime } ( x )$ . In other words, 

$$
g ^ {\prime} (x) = \lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} g _ {j} ^ {\prime} (x).
$$

Remark 9.110 In plain language, the uniform convergence of a series of continuously di¤erentiable functions yields a di¤erentiable function when the series of derivatives also converge uniformly, and the derivative of this limit function equals the sum of the derivatives of terms in the series. That is, uniform convergence of the series and its derivatives justifies di¤erentiating term by term, which means that 

$$
\left(\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} g _ {j} (x)\right) ^ {\prime} = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} g _ {j} ^ {\prime} (x).
$$

Proof Define $\begin{array} { r } { f _ { n } ( x ) = \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } g ( x ) } \end{array}$ . Then $f _ { n } ( x )$ is continuously di¤erentiable for all n as a finite sum of continuously di¤erentiable functions, and by assumption, $f _ { n } ( x ) $ $g ( x )$ uniformly. Also $\begin{array} { r } { f _ { n } ^ { \prime } ( x ) \equiv \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } g _ { j } ^ { \prime } ( x ) } \end{array}$ , and so $f _ { n } ^ { \prime } ( x )$ converges uniformly by the Cauchy criterion. The result follows from proposition 9.108 above. n 

## 9.4.2 Di¤erentiability of Power Series

We have seen that in order to have any hope of expanding a given function as a Taylor series, such a function must be infinitely di¤erentiable. However, not all infinitely di¤erentiable functions can be represented as convergent Taylor series, as 

$$
f (x) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} e ^ {- 1 / x ^ {2}}, & x \neq 0, \\ 0, & x = 0, \end{array} \right.
$$

analyzed in example 9.99 above illustrates. Here $f ^ { ( n ) } ( 0 ) = 0$ for all $n ,$ so the Taylor series centered at $x _ { 0 } = 0$ satisfies 

$$
\sum_ {j = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{j !} f ^ {(j)} (0) x ^ {j} \equiv 0,
$$

and so cannot possibly represent this function in any neighborhood of this point. 

The property of $f ( x )$ called analytic above, or more precisely, analytic in a neighborhood of $x _ { 0 } .$ , means more than just that this function is infinitely di¤erentiable at $x _ { 0 }$ . It means that the function can be represented by a Taylor series centered at $x = x _ { 0 }$ , and that this series is convergent to the function values in some neighborhood of this point. The emphasis on $^ { 6 6 } \mathrm { t o }$ the function values’’ is deliberate, since the function above has a Taylor series centered on $x _ { 0 } = 0$ that is convergent everywhere, but it does not converge to $f ( x )$ for any $x \neq 0$ 

Now a Taylor series is a special case of a power series introduced in chapter $^ { 6 , }$ and it is natural to ask: 

Question: If a function $f ( x )$ is defined as the power series $\textstyle f ( x ) = \sum _ { j = 0 } ^ { \infty } c _ { j } ( x - x _ { 0 } ) ^ { j }$ that is convergent for $| x - x _ { 0 } | < R$ for some $R > 0 \mathrm { : }$ 

1. Is $f ( x )$ infinitely di¤erentiable, and if so, how is $f ^ { ( n ) } ( x )$ evaluated? 

2. If infinitely di¤erentiable, is $f ( x )$ an analytic function in the sense of (9.30)? 

3. If an analytic function, and $f ( x )$ is expanded in a Taylor series about $x _ { 0 } ,$ , must it be the case that 

$$
c _ {n} = \frac {f ^ {(n)} (x _ {0})}{n !}?
$$

The following proposition addresses these questions, and provides a‰rmative responses. It is largely a corollary to proposition 9.109 above on series of functions, but it is stated here to clarify that a small amount of thought needs to be applied to assure that the uniformity of convergence needed for the result above applies. 

Proposition 9.111 If a function $f ( x )$ is defined by the power series 

$$
f (x) = \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {\infty} c _ {j} (x - x _ {0}) ^ {j}\tag{9.37}
$$

and has an interval of convergence given by $| x - x _ { 0 } | < R$ for some $R > 0$ , then: 

1. $f ( x )$ is infinitely di¤erentiable, and 

$$
f ^ {(n)} (x) = \sum_ {j = n} ^ {\infty} c _ {j} \frac {j !}{(j - n) !} (x - x _ {0}) ^ {j}\tag{9.38}
$$

is absolutely convergent for $\left| x - x _ { 0 } \right| < R .$ In other words, power series are infinitely differentiable and can be di¤erentiated term by term. 

2. $f ( x )$ is analytic in the sense of (9.30), so 

$$
f (x) = \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {f ^ {(n)} \left(x _ {0}\right)}{n !} \left(x - x _ {0}\right) ^ {n},
$$

and this series is absolutely convergent on $| x - x _ { 0 } | < R .$ Further 

$$
\frac {f ^ {(n)} (x _ {0})}{n !} = c _ {n}.\tag{9.39}
$$

In other words, power series expansions are unique. 

Proof Define $f _ { n } ( x )$ as the partial summation associated with $f ( x )$ : 

$$
f _ {n} (x) = \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n} c _ {j} (x - x _ {0}) ^ {j}.
$$

For the moment, assume the radius of convergence, $R < \infty$ , where we recall that R is defined in chapter 6 by $\begin{array} { r } { R = \frac { 1 } { L } } \end{array}$ , where L is given in (6.20): 

$$
L = \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {j \to \infty} \left\{\frac {| c _ {j + 1} |}{| c _ {j} |} \right\}.
$$

Then it is apparent that $f _ { n } ( x )$ is continuous, $f _ { n } ( x ) \to f ( x )$ pointwise on $| x - x _ { 0 } | < R$ and hence by exercise 30(b) converges uniformly on the compact $| x - x _ { 0 } | \le R - \epsilon$ for any $\epsilon > 0$ . Also $f _ { n } ( x )$ is di¤erentiable, 

$$
f _ {n} ^ {\prime} (x) = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} j c _ {j} (x - x _ {0}) ^ {j - 1},
$$

and we now show that $f _ { n } ^ { \prime } ( x )$ converges pointwise on $| x - x _ { 0 } | < R$ by demonstrating that the series ${ \textstyle \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { \infty } j c _ { j } ( x - x _ { 0 } ) ^ { j - 1 } }$ has the same interval of convergence as the series for $f ( x )$ . By the ratio test, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {j \to \infty} \left\{\frac {| (j + 1) c _ {j + 1} (x - x _ {0}) ^ {j} |}{| j c _ {j} (x - x _ {0}) ^ {j - 1} |} \right\} = \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {j \to \infty} \left\{\frac {j + 1}{j} \frac {| c _ {j + 1} |}{| c _ {j} |} | x - x _ {0} | \right\} \\ = \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {j \to \infty} \left\{\frac {| c _ {j + 1} |}{| c _ {j} |} \right\} | x - x _ {0} | \\ = L | x - x _ {0} |. \end{array}
$$

So the series $f _ { n } ^ { \prime } ( x )$ converges on $| x - x _ { 0 } | < R$ and hence also converges uniformly by the Cauchy criterion on $| x - x _ { 0 } | \leq R - \epsilon$ . By proposition 9.108, it follows that $f ( x )$ is di¤erentiable, and $f ^ { \prime } ( x ) = \mathrm { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } f _ { n } ^ { \prime } ( x )$ for all $| x - x _ { 0 } | \le R - \epsilon$ . Since this is true for all $\epsilon > 0$ , the result in (9.38) follows for $n = 1$ . However, $f ^ { \prime } ( x ) =$ ${ \textstyle \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { \infty } j c _ { j } ( x - x _ { 0 } ) ^ { j - 1 } }$ is now a power series to which the same argument applies, and by iteration, (9.38) follows for all n. If $R = \infty$ , the same argument applies except that compact sets needed for uniform convergence are defined, $\vert x - x _ { 0 } \vert \le R ^ { \prime }$ for any $R ^ { \prime } < \infty$ . This proves part 1 of the proposition. 

For part $^ { 2 , }$ it is apparent from (9.38) by substitution that $f ^ { ( n ) } ( x _ { 0 } ) = n ! c _ { n } ,$ and so the Taylor series centered on $x _ { 0 }$ converges absolutely for $| x - x _ { 0 } | < R$ because it is identical to the power series. n 

Remark 9.112 Of course, the notion that power series representations are unique, as stated in part 2 ofproposition 9.111, is meant in the sense that iffor some $x _ { 0 } .$ 

$$
f (x) = \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {\infty} c _ {j} (x - x _ {0}) ^ {j} = \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {\infty} d _ {j} (x - x _ {0}) ^ {j}
$$

for $| x - x _ { 0 } | < R$ with $R > 0$ , then $\begin{array} { r } { c _ { j } = d _ { j } = \frac { f ^ { ( j ) } ( x _ { 0 } ) } { j ! } } \end{array}$ for all j. A given analytic function has many Taylor series expansions for di¤erent values of $x _ { 0 }$ , of course. For example, expanding about $x = 0$ and $x = 1$ , we have 

$$
e ^ {x} = \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {x ^ {j}}{j !} = \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {e (x - 1) ^ {j}}{j !}.
$$

By the proposition above, every power series is an analytic function in its interval of convergence in the sense of definition 9.98 in section 9.3.7. 

Example 9.113 In section 7.5.1 formulas were introduced for the moment-generating function and characteristic function of a discrete random variable, and it was claimed that each was equal to a power series reflecting the moments of the given random variable. For example, $i f f ( x )$ is the probability density function ofa given discrete random variable $X : \mathcal { S } \longrightarrow \{ x _ { i } \} _ { i = 1 } ^ { \infty } \subset \mathbb { R }$ , the moment-generating function is defined by 

$$
M _ {X} (t) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\infty} e ^ {t x _ {i}} f (x _ {i}),
$$

when this series converges, and also converges absolutely, for t in an interval I about $t = 0 .$ . Now $e ^ { t x _ { i } }$ is an analytic function for all t, and expressing it as a Taylor series, we have 

$$
M _ {X} (t) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\infty} \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {(t x _ {i}) ^ {j}}{j !} f (x _ {i}).
$$

Since this series is absolutely convergent on I, we can interchange the order of summation by the analysis in section 6.1.4 to produce $( 7 . 6 4 )$ 

$$
M _ {X} (t) = \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {t ^ {j}}{j !} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\infty} x _ {i} ^ {j} f (x _ {i})
$$

$$
= \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {t ^ {j} \mu_ {j} ^ {\prime}}{j !}.
$$

As a convergent power series on $I ,$ we now have that $M _ { X } ( t )$ is infinitely di¤erentiable on $I ,$ and (9.38) can be applied to produce 

$$
M _ {X} ^ {(n)} (t) = \sum_ {j = n} ^ {\infty} \frac {t ^ {j - n} \mu_ {j} ^ {\prime}}{(j - n) !},
$$

which produces (7.65) when $t = 0$ is substituted: 

$$
\mu_ {n} ^ {\prime} = M _ {X} ^ {(n)} (0).
$$

The same analysis works for the characteristic function $C _ { X } ( t )$ , when all moments exist, and demonstrates the analogous properties of this function. As noted before, this requires the use of the power series expansion for $e ^ { i t x _ { j } }$ , with a complex exponent, and this series is seen to be absolutely convergent by the triangle inequality. However, $C _ { X } ( t )$ need not be infinitely di¤erentiable at $t = 0$ , and will have the same number of derivatives there as $f ( x )$ has moments. 

## Product of Taylor Series

The next discussion in this section relates to the product of two analytic functions. Obviously, if $f ( x )$ and $g ( x )$ are any two analytic functions, the function $h ( x ) \equiv$ $f ( x ) g ( x )$ is well defined. The question here is, if $f ( x )$ and $g ( x )$ are given as absolutely convergent Taylor series centered on $x _ { 0 } .$ , with respective radii of convergence of R and $R ^ { \prime } { \mathrm { : } }$ is $h ( x )$ analytic? If so, what is the power series representation of $h ( x )$ and what is its radius of convergence? 

The following proposition addresses this question, and expands the result in proposition 9.101, which addressed the analyticity of $a f ( x ) + b g ( x )$ for $a , b \in \mathbb { R }$ , when $f ( x )$ and $g ( x )$ are analytic. 

Proposition 9.114 Let $f ( x )$ and $g ( x )$ be analytic functions and given as convergent power series centered on x<sub>0</sub>: 

$$
f (x) = \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {f ^ {(n)} \left(x _ {0}\right)}{n !} \left(x - x _ {0}\right) ^ {n}, \quad g (x) = \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {g ^ {(n)} \left(x _ {0}\right)}{n !} \left(x - x _ {0}\right) ^ {n},
$$

which are absolutely convergent for $| x - x _ { 0 } | < R$ . Then $h ( x ) \equiv f ( x ) g ( x )$ is an analytic function, absolutely convergent for $| x - x _ { 0 } | < R .$ 

$$
h (x) = \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} d _ {n} (x - x _ {0}) ^ {n},\tag{9.40}
$$

where 

$$
d _ {n} = \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {n} \frac {f ^ {(k)} (x _ {0}) g ^ {(n - k)} (x _ {0})}{k ! (n - k) !}.\tag{9.41}
$$

Proof Because $f ( x )$ and $g ( x )$ are absolutely convergent, the conclusion follows directly from proposition 6.52. Specifically, (9.41) follows from (6.22). n 

We now have an immediate corollary from this proposition, known as the Leibniz rule for the nth-derivative of the product of two n-times di¤erentiable functions, named for Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646–1716). This corollary applies to the product of analytic functions, but is true under the weaker assumption that the functions each are simply n-times di¤erentiable. Exercise 34 assigns the proof of this formula in this general case, using mathematical induction. 

Proposition 9.115 $H f ( x )$ and $g ( x )$ are analytic functions, absolutely convergent for $| x - x _ { 0 } | < R$ , then for $h ( x ) = f ( x ) g ( x )$ 2 

$$
h ^ {(n)} (x) = \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {n} \binom {n} {k} f ^ {(k)} (x) g ^ {(n - k)} (x) \quad \text {   for   } | x - x _ {0} | <   R.\tag{9.42}
$$

Proof This formula for $h ^ { ( n ) } ( x )$ is true for $x = x _ { 0 }$ because $h ( x )$ is analytic, and hence 

$$
h (x) = \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {h ^ {(n)} (x _ {0})}{n !} (x - x _ {0}) ^ {n}.
$$

Comparing this expansion with (6.22), produces $h ^ { ( n ) } ( x _ { 0 } ) = n ! d _ { n }$ and the result follows since $\begin{array} { r } { \binom { n } { k } = \frac { n ! } { k ! ( n - k ) ! } } \end{array}$ . For any other x with $| x - x _ { 0 } | < R$ , a Taylor series can be centered on $x ,$ and will be absolutely convergent on any interval $( x - R ^ { \prime } , x + R ^ { \prime } ) \subset$ $( x _ { 0 } - R , x _ { 0 } + R )$ . With this Taylor series, and the above derivation, (9.42) follows for all such x. n 

## *Division of Taylor Series

The last discussion in this section relates to the division of two analytic functions, or the reciprocal of an analytic function. Obviously, if $f ( x )$ and $h ( x )$ are any two analytic functions, the function $\begin{array} { r } { g ( x ) \equiv \frac { h ( x ) } { f ( x ) } } \end{array}$ is well defined if $f ( x ) \neq 0$ . When $h ( x ) \equiv 1$ ， the function $g ( x )$ is the reciprocal of $f ( x )$ . The question here is, if $f ( x )$ and $h ( x )$ are given as absolutely convergent Taylor series centered on $x _ { 0 } .$ , with $f ( x _ { 0 } ) \neq 0$ , and common radius of convergence of $R ,$ is $g ( x )$ analytic? If so, what is the power series representation of $h ( x )$ and what is its radius of convergence? 

The following proposition addresses this question: 

Proposition 9.116 Let $f ( x )$ and $h ( x )$ be analytic functions and given as convergent power series centered on $x _ { 0 }$ 

$$
f (x) = \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {f ^ {(n)} \left(x _ {0}\right)}{n !} \left(x - x _ {0}\right) ^ {n}, \quad h (x) = \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {h ^ {(n)} \left(x _ {0}\right)}{n !} \left(x - x _ {0}\right) ^ {n},
$$

which are absolutely convergent for $| x - x _ { 0 } | < R$ and where $f ( x _ { 0 } ) \neq 0 .$ . Then $g ( x ) \equiv$ $\textstyle { \frac { h ( x ) } { f ( x ) } }$ is an analytic function, 

$$
g (x) = \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} c _ {n} (x - x _ {0}) ^ {n},\tag{9.43}
$$

where 

$$
c _ {0} = \frac {h (x _ {0})}{f (x _ {0})}\tag{9.44a}
$$

$$
c _ {n} = \frac {1}{f (x _ {0})} \left[ \frac {h ^ {(n)} (x _ {0})}{n !} - \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {n - 1} \frac {f ^ {(n - k)} (x _ {0}) c _ {k}}{(n - k) !} \right],\tag{9.44b}
$$

which is absolutely convergent for $\vert x - x _ { 0 } \vert < R ^ { \prime }$ for some $R ^ { \prime } > 0 .$ 

Proof Because $f ( x )$ and $h ( x )$ are absolutely convergent, the conclusion follows directly from proposition 6.53, which also showed that $\textstyle { \frac { 1 } { f ( x ) } }$ is absolutely convergent. Specifically, (9.44) follows from (6.25). n 

Remark 9.117 In section 9.8.10 below on the risk-neutral probability $q ( \Delta t )$ will be an analysis of the ratio of analytic functions and an application of this result, or equivalently, an application offormulas (6.25). However, it is often the case that the power series for the ratio can be derived directly and more easily by a ‘‘long division’’ of the power series of $h ( x )$ by the power series of $f ( x )$ rather than by generating these coe‰- cients iteratively through formulas such as in (9.44) or (6.25). The importance of the proposition above is that it assures that this ratio function is analytic in a neighborhood of x , so we can generate only a few of the terms and still be sure that the remainder will converge to 0 with the order of magnitude implied by the number of terms generated. Without such a result, we could be generating and using a partial sum of a series for which the remainder did not converge. 

Because $c _ { n } = { \frac { g ^ { ( n ) } ( x _ { 0 } ) } { n ! } }$ , we have an immediate corollary from this proposition for the nth-derivative of the ratio of two analytic functions within the interval of convergence. This corollary applies to the ratio of analytic functions because we use the result above, but is true under the general assumption that the functions are each n-times di¤erentiable, as can be proved using mathematical induction. 

Proposition 9.118 $\begin{array} { r } { I f g ( x ) \equiv \frac { h ( x ) } { f ( x ) } } \end{array}$ , with $h ( x )$ and $f ( x )$ given in proposition $9 . I I 6 ,$ then 

$$
g ^ {(n)} (x) = \frac {1}{f (x)} \left[ h ^ {(n)} (x) - \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {n - 1} \binom {n} {k} f ^ {(n - k)} (x) g ^ {(k)} (x) \right], \qquad n \geq 1.
$$

Proof This result follows from (9.44), and also follows from the Leibniz rule in (9.42) by writing $h ( x ) = f ( x ) g ( x )$ and iteratively solving for $g ^ { ( n ) } ( x )$ n 

## 9.5 Critical Point Analysis

## 9.5.1 Second-Derivative Test

With the help of section 9.3.8 on Taylor series, it is now possible to classify the critical points of a di¤erentiable function. Proposition 9.87 above provided a necessary condition in order that $x _ { 0 }$ be a relative maximum or relative minimum of $f ( x )$ namely that $f ^ { \prime } ( x _ { 0 } ) = 0$ . In other words, a necessary condition is that $x _ { 0 }$ be a critical point of $f ( x )$ . The second and higher derivatives now provide a sorting of these cases. 

Proposition 9.119 $H f ( x )$ is a twice di¤erentiable function with $f ^ { \prime } ( x _ { 0 } ) = 0 .$ , and $f ^ { \prime \prime } ( x )$ is continuous in a neighborhood ofx<sub>0</sub>, then: 

1. $x _ { 0 }$ is a relative minimum of $f ( x ) \ i f \ f ^ { \prime \prime } ( x _ { 0 } ) > 0$ 

2. $x _ { 0 }$ is a relative maximum of $f ( x ) \ i f \ f ^ { \prime \prime } ( x _ { 0 } ) < 0$

Proposition 9.124 Let $f ( x )$ be a di¤erentiable function, with $f ^ { \prime } ( x _ { 0 } ) = 0 .$ , and assume that there is an open interval I, with $x _ { 0 } \in I _ { : }$ , on which $f ^ { \prime } ( x )$ is continuous. Then:

## *9.5.2 Critical Points of Transformed Functions

When pursuing a critical point analysis of a given function $f ( x )$ , it is often convenient to first transform the function by taking a composite of $f ( x )$ with another function $g ( x )$ and consider the critical points of $g ( f ( x ) )$ . For example, if $f ( x )$ is given as an exponential function $f ( x ) = e ^ { j ( x ) }$ , it would be natural to prefer to evaluate the derivatives of ln $f ( x ) = j ( x )$ rather than derivatives of $f ( x )$ . This same idea applies when $f ( x )$ is the ratio of functions, $\begin{array} { r } { f ( x ) = \frac { j ( x ) } { k ( x ) } } \end{array}$ , or the product, $f ( x ) = j ( x ) k ( x )$ 

where again ln $f ( x )$ would be simpler to di¤erentiate than $f ( x )$ as long as the various functions are positive so that the logarithm is well defined. In these examples the function used in the composition is given by $g ( x ) = \ln x .$ 

Similar considerations apply if $f ( x )$ is given as the natural logarithm of a positive function $f ( x ) = \ln j ( x )$ , where composing with $g ( x ) = e ^ { x }$ gives $e ^ { f ( x ) } = j ( x )$ , or if $f ( x )$ is a power of a function $f ( x ) = j ( x ) ^ { a }$ ; where forming the composition with $g ( x ) = x ^ { 1 / a }$ produces a simpler function. In each case composition produces a simpler function to di¤erentiate. 

In all such cases the question is: What is the relationship between the critical points of $f ( x )$ and those of $g ( f ( x ) ) \smash { \vphantom { \big ( } 2 f ( x ) ) \smash { \mathstrut } 2 }$ The next proposition summarizes the result. 

Proposition 9.125 Let $f ( x )$ be a di¤erentiable function, and $g ( x )$ a di¤erentiable function that is well defined on $\operatorname { R n g } ( f )$ . Then, $i f x _ { 0 }$ is a critical point of $f ( x )$ , it will also be a critical point of $g ( f ( x ) )$ 

Proof The function $h ( x ) \equiv g ( f ( x ) )$ is di¤erentiable on Dmn $( f )$ , and using the results from proposition 9.76 produces 

$$
h ^ {\prime} (x) = g ^ {\prime} (f (x)) f ^ {\prime} (x).
$$

Consequently, if $\dot { { \cal f } } ^ { \prime } ( x _ { 0 } ) = 0 , \mathrm { t h e n } h ^ { \prime } ( x _ { 0 } ) = 0 .$ 

In other words, the critical points of $f ( x )$ will be a subset of the critical points of $h ( x )$ . However, we see from the formula above for $h ^ { \prime } ( x )$ that critical points of the transformed function $h ( x )$ need not be critical points of $f ( x )$ unless one knows that $g ^ { \prime } ( f ( x _ { 0 } ) ) \neq 0$ 

Example 9.126 Take $g ( x ) = e ^ { x }$ , ln x, or $x ^ { 1 / a }$ . Then $g ^ { \prime } ( x ) = e ^ { x } , { \frac { 1 } { x } }$ , and ${ \frac { 1 } { a } } x ^ { ( 1 - a ) / a } , r e -$ spectively. In the first two cases, since $g ^ { \prime } ( x )$ has no zero values, the critical points of $f ( x )$ and those of $h ( x )$ agree. In the third case of $g ( x ) = x ^ { 1 / a }$ , it appears possible for $h ( x )$ to inherit extra critical points at any value of x for which $f ( x _ { 0 } ) = 0 .$ , since then 

$$
h ^ {\prime} (x _ {0}) = g ^ {\prime} (f (x _ {0})) f ^ {\prime} (x _ {0}) = \frac {1}{a} (f (x _ {0})) ^ {(1 - a) / a} f ^ {\prime} (x _ {0}) = 0.
$$

But this conclusion requires that $\textstyle { \frac { 1 - a } { a } } > 0 .$ , which is equivalent to $\textstyle { \frac { 1 } { a } } > 1$ or $0 < a < 1$ ， since otherwise, $( 0 ) ^ { ( 1 - a ) / a }$ is meaningless. On the other hand, this transformation would typically only be considered when $f ( x ) = j ( x ) ^ { a }$ , which equals 0 only when $j ( x _ { 0 } ) = 0$ But, $i f 0 < a < 1$ , such an $f ( x )$ is not di¤erentiable when $j ( x _ { 0 } ) = 0 _ { \mathrm { { \small i } } }$ , so the di¤erentiability of $f ( x )$ assures that $j ( x _ { 0 } ) \neq 0$ and no additional critical points are inherited in this case as well. 

In summary, the three simple transformations illustrated above will exactly preserve the critical points of $f ( x )$ , as long as the di¤erentiability assumptions of the proposition are satisfied. For more general transformations, for which $g ^ { \prime } ( f ( x _ { 0 } ) ) = 0$ for some $x _ { 0 }$ , the critical points of $f ( x )$ will be augmented by the critical points of $g ( x )$ on $\operatorname { R n g } ( f )$ 

We turn next to the second derivative test: 

Proposition 9.127 Let $f ( x )$ be a twice di¤erentiable function, and $g ( x )$ a twice di¤erentiable function that is well defined on $\operatorname { R n g } ( f )$ . Then, if x<sub>0</sub> is a critical point of $f ( x )$ that is a relative maximum or relative minimum of $f ( x ) , x _ { 0 }$ will have the same property for $g ( f ( x ) ) \ i f g ^ { \prime } ( f ( x _ { 0 } ) ) > 0$ , and the opposite property $i f g ^ { \prime } ( f ( x _ { 0 } ) ) < 0 .$ 

Proof The function $h ( x ) \equiv g ( f ( x ) )$ is twice di¤erentiable on Dmn $( f )$ , and 

$$
h ^ {\prime \prime} (x) = g ^ {\prime \prime} (f (x)) [ f ^ {\prime} (x) ] ^ {2} + g ^ {\prime} (f (x)) f ^ {\prime \prime} (x).
$$

Consequently, if $f ^ { \prime } ( x _ { 0 } ) = 0$ , then 

$$
h ^ {\prime \prime} (x _ {0}) = g ^ {\prime} (f (x _ {0})) f ^ {\prime \prime} (x _ {0}),
$$

and $f ^ { \prime \prime } ( x _ { 0 } )$ and $h ^ { \prime \prime } ( x _ { 0 } )$ will have the same sign if $g ^ { \prime } ( f ( x _ { 0 } ) ) > 0$ , and opposite signs if $g ^ { \prime } ( f ( x _ { 0 } ) ) < 0$ n

$\| ( x _ { 1 } - x _ { p } , x _ { 2 } - x _ { p } , \ldots , x _ { n } - x _ { p } ) \| _ { p }$ is minimized: 

This problem can be envisioned as a problem in R or as a problem in $\mathbb { R } ^ { n } { } _ { : }$ , but we choose the former to apply the tools of this chapter. The problem then becomes

This problem was solved in chapter 3 by direct methods in the cases of $p = 1 , 2 , \infty$ ， where we recall that for $p = \infty$ the $l _ { p } { \mathrm { - n o r m } }$ problem is defined as 

Minimize: $f ( { \boldsymbol { x } } ) = \operatorname* { m a x } _ { i } \{ | x _ { i } - { \boldsymbol { x } } | \}$ 

We now return to this example for other values of $p .$ 

Example 9.129 To apply the tools of this chapter, we require $f ( x )$ to be di¤erentia-$b l e ,$ and we have seen in example $9 . 8 0$ (case 8) that this requires that $1 < p < \infty$ $B e \mathrm { - }$ cause $g ( x ) = x ^ { p }$ is an increasing function, the maximums and minimums $o f f ( x )$ and $f ( x ) ^ { p }$ agree as noted in example 9.128 above, with ${ \frac { 1 } { a } } = p .$ This follows because $f ( x ) > 0$ for all x except in the trivial case where all $x _ { j } = c _ { s }$ and so $f ( c ) = 0 .$ . We ignore this case, since then $x _ { p } = c$ apparently. 

Suppose that $\{ x _ { j } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { n }$ contain m di¤erent values, which we denote by $\{ y _ { j } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { m }$ in increasing order, and that the original set contains $n _ { j }$ of each $y _ { j }$ . The goal is then to find the minimum of $h ( x ) = g ( f ( x ) )$ 

$$
h (x) = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {m} n _ {j} | y _ {j} - x | ^ {p}, \quad 1 <   p <   \infty .

From (9.20), we have that 

$$
h ^ {\prime} (x) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} - p \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {m} n _ {j} (y _ {j} - x) ^ {p - 1}, & x \leq y _ {1}, \\ p \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {k} n _ {j} (x - y _ {j}) ^ {p - 1} - p \sum_ {j = k + 1} ^ {m} n _ {j} (y _ {j} - x) ^ {p - 1}, & y _ {k} \leq x \leq y _ {k + 1}, \\ p \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {m} n _ {j} (x - y _ {j}) ^ {p - 1}, & y _ {m} \leq x. \end{array} \right.
$$

Note that $h ^ { \prime } ( x )$ is continuous, since its values at the interval endpoints $\{ y _ { j } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { m }$ are well defined even though they are defined piecewise continuously on intervals. Also $h ^ { \prime } ( x )$ is negative for $x \leq y _ { 1 }$ and positive for $y _ { m } \leq x .$ So by the intermediate value theorem, there is at least one point $x ^ { \prime } { } _ { i }$ with 

$$
y _ {1} <   x ^ {\prime} <   y _ {m} \quad a n d \quad h ^ {\prime} (x ^ {\prime}) = 0.
$$

Specifically, if $y _ { k } \leq x ^ { \prime } \leq y _ { k + 1 }$ , then

$$

When $p = 2 ,$ , this equation can be explicitly solved, producing

as derived in chapter 3.

This is apparent for $x \leq y _ { 1 }$ and $y _ { m } \leq x$ but also for $y _ { k } \leq x \leq$ $y _ { k + 1 }$ , since as x increases, the positive summation increases and the negative summation decreases. Note that in general, we can not use a second derivative test to confirm that $x ^ { \prime }$ is a minimum, since $h ^ { \prime } ( x )$ is di¤erentiable only if $p \geq 2 .$ . If we assume that $p \geq 2$ , or $j f 1 < p < 2$ and $x ^ { \prime } \neq y _ { j }$ for any $j ,$ then the second derivative test can be used:

## 9.6 Concave and Convex Functions

## 9.6.1 Definitions

In previous chapters the notions of convexity and concavity have been encountered. First we recall the definitions: 

Definition 9.130 A function $f ( x )$ is concave on an interval I, which can be open, closed or semi-closed, finite or infinite, iffor any $x , y \in I$ 5 

$$
f (t x + (1 - t) y) \geq t f (x) + (1 - t) f (y) \quad \text {   for   } t \in [ 0, 1 ].\tag{9.45}
$$

A function $f ( x )$ is convex on I if, for any $x , y \in I ,$ 

$$
f (t x + (1 - t) y) \leq t f (x) + (1 - t) f (y) \quad \text {   for   } t \in [ 0, 1 ].\tag{9.46}
$$

When the inequalities are strict for $t \in ( 0 , 1 )$ , such functions are referred to as strictly concave and strictly convex, respectively. 

Remark 9.131 Note that $f ( x )$ is concave if and only $i f - f ( x )$ is convex, and conversely. Consequently most propositions need only be proved in one case, and the other case will follow once the e¤ect of the minus sign on the result is reflected. 

Interestingly, the properties of concavity and convexity are quite strong. As it turns out, concave and convex functions are always continuous on open intervals and are in fact Lipschitz continuous. 

Proposition 9.132 $H f ( x )$ is concave or convex on an open interval I, then it is Lipschitz continuous on I. 

Proof We demonstrate this for a convex function $f ( x )$ . Then, if $g ( x )$ is concave, the result follows from the continuity of the convex $- g ( x )$ . To this end, let $y \in I$ be given, and let $\boldsymbol { J } = \left( y - a , y + a \right)$ be defined so that $[ y - a , y + a ] \subset I$ Since I is open, there is an open interval about y contained in I by definition, and we simply choose a smaller open interval J whose closure is also in I. Let $M = \operatorname* { m a x } ( f ( y - a )$ $f ( \boldsymbol { y } + \boldsymbol { a } ) )$ . For any $x \in J ,$ we conclude that $f ( x ) \leq M ,$ , since any such point can be expressed $x = ( 1 - t ) ( y - a ) + t ( y + a )$ for some $t \in ( 0 , 1 )$ , and since $f ( x )$ is convex, $( 9 . 4 6 )$ provides this conclusion. Now let $x \in J$ be given and assume for the moment that $x \geq y$ . To standardize notation, let $x = y + t a$ for some $t \in [ 0 , 1 ]$ , then we have that 

$$
y - a <   y \leq x \equiv y + t a <   y + a.
$$

Now, by construction, 

$$
x = (1 - t) y + t (y + a).
$$

In order to write x as a linear combination of $y - a$ and this same y, an algebraic exercise produces 

$$
y = \frac {t}{1 + t} (y - a) + \frac {1}{1 + t} x,
$$

where both $\textstyle { \frac { t } { 1 + t } } , { \frac { 1 } { 1 + t } } \in [ 0 , 1 ]$ . Now, from the convexity of $f ( x )$ , and the definition of M, we conclude that 

$$
f (x) \leq (1 - t) f (y) + t M,
$$

$$
f (y) \leq \frac {t}{1 + t} M + \frac {1}{1 + t} f (x).
$$

Using the first inequality for an upper bound, the second for the lower bound, provides 

$$
- t [ M - f (y) ] \leq f (x) - f (y) \leq t [ M - f (y) ].
$$

That is, 

$$
| f (x) - f (y) | \leq t | M - f (y) |.
$$

Since $\begin{array} { r } { t = \frac { x - y } { a } } \end{array}$ , we have the final result for Lipschitz continuity: 

$$
| f (x) - f (y) | \leq \frac {| M - f (y) |}{a} (x - y) \quad \text {   for   } x \geq y.
$$

An identical construction applies when $x \leq y ,$ by expressing $x = y - t a ,$ so $y - a <$ $x \leq y < y + a .$ Combining the resulting inequalities, we get 

$$
| f (x) - f (y) | \leq C | x - y |.
$$

Example 9.133 It is important to note that this proposition does not extend to the result that a convex/concave function on a closed interval is continuous. For example, on the interval ½0; 1, define 

$$
f (x) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} x (x - 1), & 0 <   x \leq 1, \\ - 1, & x = 0. \end{array} \right.
$$

Then $f ( x )$ is apparently concave, and equally apparently, not continuous. 

When a function is di¤erentiable, it is relatively easy to confirm when it is either concave or convex. 

Proposition 9.134 There are two derivatives-based tests that characterize convexity and concavity: 

1. $H f ( x )$ is di¤erentiable, then: 

(a) fðxÞ is concave on an interval if and only $i f f ^ { \prime } ( x )$ is a decreasing function on that interval. 

(b) $f ( x )$ is convex on an interval if and only $i f f ^ { \prime } ( x )$ is an increasing function on that interval. 

(c) fðxÞ is strictly concave i¤ $f ^ { \prime } ( x )$ is strictly decreasing, and strictly convex $i f f ^ { \prime } ( x )$ is strictly increasing. 

2. $H f ( x )$ is twice di¤erentiable, then: 

(a) fðxÞ is concave on an interval if and only $i f f ^ { \prime \prime } ( x ) \leq 0$ on that interval. 

(b) fðxÞ is convex on an interval ifand only $i f f ^ { \prime \prime } ( x ) \geq 0$ on that interval. 

(c) Strict concavity and strict convexity follow from $f ^ { \prime \prime } ( x ) < 0 _ { \ast }$ , or $f ^ { \prime \prime } ( x ) > 0 .$ respectively.

Substituting back the original functions produces 

$$
f (t x + (1 - t) y) = f (y) + t (x - y) f ^ {\prime} \left(y + \theta_ {1} (x - y)\right),
$$

$$
f (t x + (1 - t) y) = f (x) + (t - 1) (x - y) f ^ {\prime} \left(y + \theta_ {2} (x - y)\right).
$$

Next, multiplying the first equation by $1 - t$ and the second by t and adding produces 

$$
f (t x + (1 - t) y) = (1 - t) f (y) + t f (x) + E (t)
$$

where the error function is defined as 

$$
E (t) = (x - y) t (1 - t) \left[ f ^ {\prime} \left(y + \theta_ {1} (x - y)\right) - f ^ {\prime} \left(y + \theta_ {2} (x - y)\right) \right].
$$

To investigate the sign of $E ( t )$ , recall $y < x .$ . So the sign of $E ( t )$ is the same as the sign of the term in square brackets. Now since $\theta _ { 1 } < \theta _ { 2 }$ by construction, $y + \theta _ { 1 } ( x - y )$ $< y + \theta _ { 2 } ( x - y )$ and we conclude that: 

$E ( t ) \geq 0 \mathrm { i f f } f ^ { \prime } ( x )$ is decreasing, and then $f ( x )$ is concave, 

$E ( t ) \leq 0 \mathrm { i f f } f ^ { \prime } ( x )$ is increasing, and then fðxÞ is convex. 

If $f ^ { \prime } ( x )$ is strictly monotonic, then $f ( x )$ is either strictly concave or strictly convex, since then $E ( t ) > 0$ or $E ( t ) < 0$ , respectively. 

2. Turning next to twice di¤erentiable $f ( x )$ , let $y < x$ be given. Applying (9.33) to $f ^ { \prime } ( x )$ with $n = 0$ , and $x _ { 0 } = y$ , we get 

$$
f ^ {\prime} (x) = f ^ {\prime} (y) + (x - y) f ^ {\prime \prime} (\theta), \qquad y <   \theta <   x.
$$

Now, if $f ^ { \prime \prime } ( \theta ) \leq 0 .$ , for all $\theta ,$ it is apparent that $f ^ { \prime } ( x ) \leq f ^ { \prime } ( y )$ , and hence $f ^ { \prime } ( x )$ is a decreasing function and $f ( x )$ is concave by part 1. Similarly, if $f ^ { \prime \prime } ( \theta ) \geq 0$ , we conclude that $f ( x )$ is convex. 

So the restrictions on $f ^ { \prime \prime } ( x )$ in parts $2 ( \mathrm { a } )$ and 2(b) assure concavity and convexity. To demonstrate that these restrictions on $f ^ { \prime \prime } ( x )$ are assured by the assumptions of convavity or convexity, we argue the concavity result by contradiction, and the convexity result is identical. Assume that $f ( x )$ is concave on an interval and that there is some x in the interval with $f ^ { \prime \prime } ( x ) > 0$ . Then 

$$
\lim _ {t \to 0} \frac {f ^ {\prime} (x + t) - f ^ {\prime} (x)}{t} > 0.
$$

By definition of limit, we conclude that there exists $\epsilon > 0$ so that ${ \frac { f ^ { \prime } ( x + t ) - f ^ { \prime } ( x ) } { t } } > 0$ for $| t | < \epsilon$ . Hence, taking $0 < t < \epsilon ,$ we conclude that 

$$
f ^ {\prime} (x + t) > f ^ {\prime} (x).
$$

So $f ^ { \prime } ( x )$ is a strictly increasing function on $[ x , x + \epsilon )$ , contradicting the concavity of $f ( x )$ by part $1 ( \mathrm { a } )$ 

Finally, for part $2 ( \mathrm { c } )$ if $f ^ { \prime \prime } ( \theta ) < 0$ or $f ^ { \prime \prime } ( \theta ) > 0$ for all $\theta ,$ then strict concavity (respectively, strict convexity) is assured by the identity above between $f ^ { \prime } ( x )$ and $f ^ { \prime } ( y )$ for $y < x$ n

Returning to the discussion on points of inflection, we begin with a definition. 

Definition 9.137 A point $x _ { 0 }$ is a point ofinflection of $f ( x )$ ifthere is an interval $( a , b )$ containing $x _ { 0 }$ so that $f ( x )$ is concave on $( a , x _ { 0 } )$ and convex on $( x _ { 0 } , b )$ , or conversely. 

Example 9.138 The point $x = 0$ is a point of inflection of $f ( x ) = x ^ { 3 } .$ , since $f ^ { \prime \prime } ( x ) =$ $6 x ,$ which is positive for $x > 0$ , and hence $f ( x )$ is convex on $( 0 , \infty )$ . Also $f ^ { \prime \prime } ( x )$ is negative for $x < 0$ , and so $f ( x )$ is concave on $( - \infty , 0 )$ . For this example, $f ^ { \prime } ( x ) = 0 .$ , so $x = 0$ is also a critical point. But inflection points need not be critical points. For example, $g ( x ) = x ^ { 3 } + b x$ satisfies $g ^ { \prime \prime } ( x ) = 6 x ,$ , so $x = 0$ is again an inflection point, and yet $g ^ { \prime } ( 0 ) = b$ can be any value we choose. 

In the same way that potential relative maximums and minimums can be identified by inspecting the critical points of a function where $f ^ { \prime } ( x ) = 0$ , there is a necessary condition in order for a point to be a point of inflection. 

Proposition 9.139 $I f x _ { 0 }$ is a point of inflection of a twice di¤erentiable function $f ( x )$ with $f ^ { \prime \prime } ( x )$ continuous, then $f ^ { \prime \prime } ( x _ { 0 } ) = 0 .$ 

Proof This follows immediately from proposition 9.134 above, since a twice di¤erentiable function satisfies $f ^ { \prime \prime } ( x ) \leq 0$ when concave and $f ^ { \prime \prime } ( x ) \geq 0$ when convex. 

Since $f ^ { \prime \prime } ( x )$ is continuous, $f ^ { \prime \prime } ( x _ { 0 } ) = \operatorname* { l i m } _ { x \to x _ { 0 } } f ( x )$ , and this common value must therefore be 0. n 

Example 9.140 As noted in section 9.5.1, functions of the form, $f ( x ) = a x ^ { n }$ , for integer $n > 2 ,$ and $a \in \mathbb { R }$ , provide a variety of possible behaviors when $f ^ { \prime \prime } ( 0 ) = 0$ . For n even, it is apparent that $x _ { 0 } = 0$ is a relative minimum $i f a > 0 .$ , and a relative maximum if $a < 0$ . For n odd, it is also apparent that for $a > 0$ , the second derivative satisfies $f ^ { \prime \prime } ( x ) > 0$ for $x > 0$ and conversely for $x < 0$ . Hence $x _ { 0 } = 0$ is a point in inflection. The same conclusion is reached for $a < 0$ 

More generally, as noted in remark 9.123, $i f f ( x )$ is a function with $f ^ { ( j ) } ( x _ { 0 } ) = 0$ for $j = 1 , \ldots , n - 1$ , and $f ^ { ( n ) } ( x _ { 0 } ) \neq 0 .$ , with $f ^ { ( n ) } ( x )$ continuous, then if n is even, $x _ { 0 }$ will be a relative minimum if $f ^ { ( n ) } ( x _ { 0 } ) > 0$ and a relative maximum if $f ^ { ( n ) } ( x _ { 0 } ) < 0 .$ . $$
f (x) = f \left(x _ {0}\right) + \frac {1}{n !} f ^ {(n)} (y) \left(x - x _ {0}\right) ^ {n},

where y is between x and $x _ { 0 } .$ .
